explanation: Builds a fairness argument from concrete contract mechanics, though 'arbitrarily' and 'what operators want' are assertions.

text: I do have concern that we have just seen this House pass the online gambling bill, where the definitions in that bill were archaic. They did not include any of the things that would be captured that have just been expressed. That bill creates and expands an online digital gaming market, and it encourages competitiveness, which we have not seen before in New Zealand.
explanation: Draws a pointed consistency argument — bipartisan harm-reduction talk alongside a bill she says expands a harmful market; specific, though the 'archaic definitions' claim is asserted.

text: There is no silver bullet, as has been expressed. A blanket ban sends a good signal and may have some help, but really, we need a multi-layered approach... We need education, we need prevention, we need peer support, we need accessible youth mental health care, and we need the platforms to take responsibility for the environments that they create.
explanation: Acknowledges a ban's limited utility and lays out a coherent multi-pronged response rather than a single fix.

text: One of them reports in its 2025 annual report that it has $600 million worth of undrawn debt capacity—in other words, that's the capacity of the retirement village residents' money—but also they have 27 percent of uncommitted arrays in stock and also 31 percent of a contract pipeline increase.
explanation: Uses operator financial disclosures to rebut the Minister's liquidity argument — evidence-based reasoning.

text: Mr Carter himself was a man of great integrity and known in his community as being a really honourable person, but he did, through his endeavours, get tens of thousands of dollars and then left this really useful legacy... All of those things can be true at the same time.
explanation: Holds competing truths together without false dichotomy—nuanced reasoning about a complicated legacy.

text: In the design of that, you are required to identify who are Māori and to have a consultation with, roughly, one-fifth—20 percent—of your population. Now, I ask you whether that is practical, and whether that is a reasonable thing to do.
explanation: Conflates a duty to consult Māori with an obligation to individually consult every person of Māori whakapapa, inflating it to '20 percent of the population' — a strawman that misrepresents how consultation works.

text: The question, Minister, is why it is that, at the moment, it appears, you are not supporting this amendment, because it would be consistent with the coalition agreement to support the amendment.
explanation: Argues the amendment follows from a stated coalition principle; reasoning is clear but rests on the agreement rather than transport evidence.

text: Yeah, the Auditor-General should have picked that up—absolutely. Lots of people should have picked that up, but we haven't, and that is one of the reasons we have an infrastructure deficit which looks as it does.
explanation: Links oversight failure to the infrastructure deficit, but the causal claim is asserted rather than evidenced.

text: Two million, 1.6 million, 1.4 million—these are theoretical houses. They are the houses that conceivably could be built under a set of planning rules, but they are not the houses that will be built.
explanation: Draws a clear, valid distinction between zoning-enabled capacity and actual delivery.

text: We asked them that question: "What proportion of the costs of growth are paid for by that growth?" ... And they said, "Rough order of magnitude: 30 to 50 percent." That means that 50 to 70 percent is paid for by existing ratepayers, existing taxpayers, existing consumers. Growth is not paying for growth.
explanation: Evidence-based: cites the Infrastructure Commission's testimony and draws the arithmetic conclusion that follows.

text: It’s really important that we work together across the House to have a orderly pipeline for those investments that need to be made so that we can continue to do that for the future.
explanation: Direction (orderly investment pipeline) but no amounts, named projects, or timing.

text: This bill is about reducing the compliance burden for making simple transactions and lending; for people to get on and get things done that they want. This is a practical and responsible bill, and I commend it to the House.
explanation: States the bill's general purpose (reducing compliance burden) but offers no figures, mechanisms, or named provisions.

text: National is strengthening and helping to shore up the future by increasing the default payments for KiwiSaver, for example—that’s one of the things that we will be doing.
explanation: Names a real mechanism (KiwiSaver default payments) but no rate, amount, or date.

text: if there are new changes to the immigration instructions that happen while somebody is having their application for residence looked at that would be beneficial to them, then that is automatically applied to their application. I think that that is a very sensible change, and I commend the bill to the House.
explanation: Identifies a precise mechanism (beneficial instruction changes auto-applied to pending residence applications).

text: These systems continuously harvest that data. They harvest the information about what a young person watches, what they pause on, what they replay, what they comment on, what keeps them online longer, and then the system feeds them more of it. That’s algorithmic amplification. It’s concerning because that’s not necessarily optimised for truth or balance or resilience or healthy development; it’s optimised for attention. And what gets attention is what gets advertising revenue, and emotionally charged material is exceptionally effective at capturing attention.
explanation: Describes concrete mechanisms (data harvesting, amplification, attention-optimisation) rather than slogans.

text: We’d be interested to explore if there’s any scope for the trust to support local residences, businesses, and groups with energy independence, for example, through initiatives such as solar power.
explanation: Names a concrete idea (solar power, energy independence) but only as something to ‘explore’, no commitment or detail.

text: Given what we know from this piece of legislation, that it allows the Minister to sell off—or get rid of; sorry—conservation land as he sees fit, it gives the Minister a heck of a lot of powers and all New Zealanders should be concerned.
explanation: Names an alleged power but vaguely ('a heck of a lot of powers') without citing the clause.

text: they’ve got $1 million that they’re putting into solar on schools, marae, and council buildings.
explanation: Concrete figure ($1m) and named recipients (schools, marae, council buildings).

text: 200,000 households in 2025 were not able to keep their homes adequately warm; 160,000 households could not pay electricity, gas, rates, or water bills on time more than once in the last 12 months; over 160,000 households put up with a cold house to keep costs down; and 100,000 households suffered dampness and mould.
explanation: Multiple precise household counts with a timeframe.

text: This Government has already cut $178 million of funding from the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority, which provided funding for hot-water heating, low-cost energy-efficiency measures, an LED lighting scheme
explanation: Names the amount, the agency, and the affected programmes.

text: They're delivering electricity to power 13,000 Kiwi homes, as well as geothermal process heat for the Kawerau Industrial Complex.
explanation: Names the project, the household count, and the industrial heat use.

text: Here are the three steps we need to take: we need to overcome the political inertia to fix the broken electricity market... We need to support grid-scale renewables for households, communities, and iwi... And we need to beef up energy conservation
explanation: Lays out three named directions but without figures, mechanisms, or timeframes for delivery.

text: They want no congestion. They want to be able to use a good public transport system. Those things affect all of us. They affect all people, regardless of whether they are Māori or whether they are non-Māori.
explanation: General aspiration about wanting good transport, no mechanism or measure.

text: Now, Māori, actually, it doesn’t even say it’s in Auckland. Essentially, it could be one fifth of the entire population of New Zealand. In fact, it doesn’t even say you’ve got to be in New Zealand.
explanation: Concrete in scoping the term's potential breadth, but the consultation context he later concedes (public stage captures all Māori) qualifies it.

text: If we mean iwi, we should be saying iwi; if we mean Māori, it’s a very, very large number of people. As I said, roughly one in five New Zealanders, we are told, have some element of Māori whakapapa
explanation: Quantifies the concern ('one in five') and distinguishes 'iwi' from 'Māori' as drafting alternatives.

text: It has taken us 183 years to get to the point of having 612,000 houses—612,000 houses. The numbers we’re talking about over the next 30 years… are way beyond what has been delivered in all the history of Auckland City.
explanation: Names exact stock (612,000), the 183-year span, and 30-year horizon.

text: the trust now has more than $200 million dollars in assets—$207 million, according to the annual report, but $173 million of that is essentially the ownership of the lines network that is there.
explanation: Exact dollar figures and breakdown of the asset base.

text: This is something that has been a failure of all sides of this House—it’s not one party or the other.
explanation: Accepts shared blame across parties rather than scoring points; builds common ground.

text: It’s really important that we work together across the House to have a orderly pipeline for those investments that need to be made so that we can continue to do that for the future.
explanation: Explicit cross-party, consensus-seeking call for a bipartisan infrastructure pipeline.

text: This bill has had very wide support across the House, and I also add my support.
explanation: Notes cross-House agreement, but is a brief endorsement rather than an active attempt to build consensus.

text: The reality is that National has no plan, and that’s why they’re just yelling a lot, because they think that if they yell a lot, New Zealanders won’t notice that they absolutely have no plan at all.
explanation: Combative rallying of her own side; no attempt to persuade across the aisle.

text: In a time when partisanship can often overshadow progress, it’s great to see a sense of unity and a shared commitment to Carterton’s future by supporting this bill.
explanation: Explicitly welcomes cross-party unity and shared purpose.

text: National is committed to constructive change. We believe that if the bill, however, does not undergo real, meaningful improvements during the select committee stage, we will not be able to support it beyond that point.
explanation: Constructive, conditional framing that signals openness rather than combativeness.

text: We must work together to protect our marine resources for future generations.
explanation: Unifying call to common purpose.

text: At the end of the day, we are the adults and we have a responsibility to do everything in our power to protect our children as best as we can.
explanation: Inclusive, responsibility-framed appeal, though general.

text: Mr Carter himself was a man of great integrity and known in his community as being a really honourable person, but he did, through his endeavours, get tens of thousands of dollars and then left this really useful legacy... All of those things can be true at the same time.
explanation: Bridges perspectives, inviting a shared, nuanced view across the House.

text: We’d be interested to explore if there’s any scope for the trust to support local residences, businesses, and groups with energy independence, for example, through initiatives such as solar power.
explanation: Constructive, collaborative suggestion aimed at the select-committee process.

text: We heard a member opposite talking about tourists having to pay to partake in the beauty of New Zealand’s nature—and, sure, I don’t disagree with that, so long as that money is spent on the upkeep of things like tracks, protecting our native species and areas, not funding restaurants and wine bars in the most pristine areas of our conservation estate.
explanation: Concedes common ground with the other side (charging tourists) before drawing a conditional line.

text: When we came into Government, it was clear that the culture that had been inculcated through the Government Public Service was profligate, it was irresponsible, and it wasn’t even putting in basic, fundamental, profit-and-loss, balance-sheet sort of stuff that I’d expect as a governor.
explanation: Sweeping pejorative characterisation (‘profligate’, ‘irresponsible’) of the public service rather than a specific, substantiated critique.

text: One of the very disappointing things for me about the last Government was that they had the mandate. They had an absolute majority, which was a rare thing in this Parliament under MMP, and yet they didn’t address the things that we’ve seen coming for decades.
explanation: Pointed criticism of the previous government’s record but aimed at inaction on policy, not personal attack.

text: I lived through the 1990s National Party “mother of all Budgets” welfare reform, and I don’t think any of us have got an appetite to be doing major reform on the welfare system, just carte blanche cutting benefits.
explanation: Acknowledges the human cost of past cuts without attacking opponents.

text: As other members have said, they’re addicted to social media, well, I admit that I have suffered that addiction, as well.
explanation: Candid and self-deprecating, lowers the temperature of the debate.

text: This is something that has been a failure of all sides of this House—it’s not one party or the other.
explanation: Non-partisan framing, no personal attack, focuses on collective policy failure.

text: a person whose only job has been in politics and who has managed, basically, an "F" in every portfolio he has managed. Let's go through his performance: Police—under his watch, crime went up; the Public Service—numbers went up; Education—outcomes went down; COVID-19—he locked New Zealanders out of this country
explanation: Sustained personal attack on Chris Hipkins' competence and career rather than engaging policy.

text: He hasn't read the bill. He called it the “Consumer Commission”; no, it's the Commerce Commission, firstly, and then, secondly, he talked about the FMCA—there's no FMCA, and if the member checks the Hansard, he'll realise he hasn't actually read the bill.
explanation: Repeated assertion that the opponent 'hasn't read the bill' is a personal jab at his competence/diligence, though anchored to specific claimed errors.

text: The quality of the debt is also important: about infrastructure, economic growth, things that power our economy out, not pet projects like the other side did when they were in Government.
explanation: ‘Pet projects’ is a dismissive jab at the opposition’s spending rather than a specified, substantiated critique.

text: There are bills of consequence in this Parliament, bills where you think, “This is why I came to this House.” Sadly, this is not one of those bills, but I do wish to acknowledge that it is an anon-nomoly.
explanation: Dismisses the bill's importance but does so good-naturedly and still acknowledges the member who brought it — no personal attack.

text: I wish to thank Mayor Wayne Brown, Minister Simeon Brown, transport Minister Chris Bishop, and my select committee colleagues on the Transport and Infrastructure Committee for a wonderful select committee process.
explanation: Gracious thanks to colleagues and the process; respectful in tone.

text: it couldn’t get any more vivid as a picture to be cancelling a national resilience fund and handing out buckets of KFC. I mean, how short term can you get it?
explanation: Sensationalist ‘buckets of KFC’ mockery used as a cheap shot rather than engaging the policy substance.

text: National’s answers are property speculation. They are to sell off our assets; to look at overseas investments; and also mentioned is to promise roads that aren’t funded and don’t have a source of income; and offer things like $2.9 billion of tax cuts and additional millions of dollars for tobacco companies.
explanation: Largely attacks the opponent’s agenda; ‘additional millions for tobacco companies’ is a loaded characterisation, though most items target policy not person.

text: Does she think it was the right use of Government money to be giving a significant amount, undisclosed, for, for example, Robbie Williams to come to Auckland when people in her own electorate aren't being given adequate support by the Ministry of Social Development to be able to retrain and to get the support, and those on the ground unemployed are not receiving adequate support?
explanation: A pointed juxtaposition aimed at the Minister's own electorate, but framed as a spending-priorities question rather than a personal insult.

text: How can she claim that, when she slashed funding to the mayor’s task force for jobs and now there are almost 28,000 fewer 15- to 24-year-olds in work compared to two years ago?
explanation: Pointed and accusatory ('slashed') but focused on policy and outcomes, not the person.

text: My question to the Minister is: did she get her priorities right in the Budget, given the record levels of job losses that New Zealanders have sustained right across the regions?
explanation: Critical but legitimate question focused on Budget priorities and outcomes, not character.

text: In a time when partisanship can often overshadow progress, it’s great to see a sense of unity and a shared commitment to Carterton’s future by supporting this bill.
explanation: Gracious, collaborative tone with no attacks.

text: I asked the Associate Minister Tama Potaka about this in the House yesterday, and his reasons for failing seniors were limp.
explanation: 'Failing seniors' and 'limp' frame the Minister dismissively, though tied to his stated reasons.

text: Many of the seniors got as much as $2.15 a week in the Government's tax package.
explanation: Pointed criticism of the tax package's impact, focused on the policy outcome.

text: I do have concern that we have just seen this House pass the online gambling bill, where the definitions in that bill were archaic. They did not include any of the things that would be captured that have just been expressed. That bill creates and expands an online digital gaming market, and it encourages competitiveness, which we have not seen before in New Zealand.
explanation: Sharp criticism aimed at legislation and its substance, not personal attack.

text: how is that fair to existing residents when they're going to be worse off? ... if a vast number of New Zealanders see three months as a fairer repayment time, which is in my member's bill, would he consider reducing the repayment time, given that he seems to have arbitrarily chosen one year, which is what the operators want
explanation: Sharp but policy-focused, engaging the substance of the proposed law.

text: I am curious to know whether the member has researched that and has satisfied himself that he's really comfortable with what happened at that period... I know that when we were speaking about this previously in the House, there may have been some sensitivities for some of those who were in the Parliament listening to a farewell speech from one of our Māori colleagues.
explanation: Raises a sensitive historical question carefully and respectfully, explicitly disclaiming any accusation about the will itself.

text: one big mistake the Government made was killing off the community energy fund. Now we’re looking to the sector to provide that, and Horizon Trust is looking to do just that.
explanation: Direct criticism of a specific government decision (scrapping the community energy fund), focused on policy not person.

text: The Government is forcing extreme hardship on Kiwis by prioritising fossil fuels, which they should know by now creates high power prices and drives extreme weather events, just like Wellington suffered last week, and the Far North the week before, and Ōtepoti before that.
explanation: Pointed criticism of policy, but the 'forcing extreme hardship' framing edges into attributing bad intent.

text: This Government is flailing about. They haven't just run out of fuel; they've run out of ideas, and they hope that we don't notice before 7 November.
explanation: Rhetorical jab ('run out of ideas') — mild and pun-based rather than a personal attack.

text: National is strengthening and helping to shore up the future by increasing the default payments for KiwiSaver, for example—that’s one of the things that we will be doing.
explanation: Claims a concrete policy (raising KiwiSaver default contributions) but framed as ‘will be doing’—intent/in-progress rather than demonstrated delivery.

text: Michael Cullen in KiwiSaver is a big promise in terms of how we deliver on that, and KiwiSaver has been a critical part of how we do that. I’m incredibly proud that that was delivered by a previous Labour Government.
explanation: Claims credit for KiwiSaver, a concrete policy that was actually designed and implemented under the previous Labour government—delivered, not just promised.

text: When I asked repeatedly, at the committee stage, the Minister of Internal Affairs to explain the harm minimisation elements of the bill, she did not seem to know the difference between harm minimisation and consumer protection.
explanation: A one-sided characterisation of an exchange the listener cannot verify; 'did not seem to know' editorialises.

text: food prices are up around 9 percent since this Government took office.
explanation: A specific, checkable inflation figure; plausible but unverified here.

text: Many of the seniors got as much as $2.15 a week in the Government's tax package.
explanation: A specific figure used to characterise the tax package's effect on seniors; broadly plausible but contestable as a representative figure.

text: One of them reports in its 2025 annual report that it has $600 million worth of undrawn debt capacity—in other words, that's the capacity of the retirement village residents' money—but also they have 27 percent of uncommitted arrays in stock and also 31 percent of a contract pipeline increase.
explanation: Specific figures attributed to a published report; plausible but unverified here.

text: we cannot look at this bill without acknowledging that this was during a colonial era when a lot of Māori land was taken through unfair contract terms, unequal bargaining power, and pressure on Māori landowners.
explanation: Accurate historical characterisation of 19th-century Māori land alienation in the Wairarapa era.

text: one big mistake the Government made was killing off the community energy fund. Now we’re looking to the sector to provide that, and Horizon Trust is looking to do just that.
explanation: References a real policy change; the ‘mistake’ judgement is opinion but the factual basis is plausible.

text: 200,000 households in 2025 were not able to keep their homes adequately warm; 160,000 households could not pay electricity, gas, rates, or water bills on time more than once in the last 12 months; over 160,000 households put up with a cold house to keep costs down; and 100,000 households suffered dampness and mould.
explanation: Detailed figures attributed to a Hidden Energy Hardship hui; plausible and sourced, unverified here.

text: This Government has already cut $178 million of funding from the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority, which provided funding for hot-water heating, low-cost energy-efficiency measures, an LED lighting scheme
explanation: Specific dollar figure and named agency; consistent with reported EECA budget cuts, plausible.

text: They're delivering electricity to power 13,000 Kiwi homes, as well as geothermal process heat for the Kawerau Industrial Complex.
explanation: Concrete claim about the TOPP2 geothermal station he personally attended; specific and plausible.

text: In the design of that, you are required to identify who are Māori and to have a consultation with, roughly, one-fifth—20 percent—of your population. Now, I ask you whether that is practical, and whether that is a reasonable thing to do.
explanation: The 'one in five with Māori whakapapa' figure is roughly defensible, but using it to imply consulting 250,000+ individuals is misleading.

text: there’s only so far that you can push costs down before builders say, “Actually, it’s not worth it. I can’t make a dollar out of it.”, and they won’t build… in the COVID situation, we saw prices ramp up very, very fast; we saw development ramp up very, very fast; and then the market turned… development dropped down as the prices dropped down.
explanation: Accurately describes the boom-then-slowdown in construction activity following the pandemic price cycle.

text: If we mean iwi, we should be saying iwi; if we mean Māori, it’s a very, very large number of people. As I said, roughly one in five New Zealanders, we are told, have some element of Māori whakapapa
explanation: The 'roughly one in five' figure is close to the actual share of NZ with Māori descent (~17–19%); appropriately hedged with 'we are told'.

text: growth, by and large, is not driven by births and deaths now; it is driven by migration.
explanation: Accurate — net migration is the dominant driver of NZ population growth in recent years.

text: That growth is no longer being delivered by births being greater than deaths, because we know, actually, that we’re now at less than replacement level. It’s being delivered by migration.
explanation: NZ's fertility rate is below replacement and population growth is migration-driven—both accurate.

text: Michael Cullen in KiwiSaver is a big promise in terms of how we deliver on that, and KiwiSaver has been a critical part of how we do that. I’m incredibly proud that that was delivered by a previous Labour Government.
explanation: Long-term-savings advocacy backed by Labour’s actual record of establishing KiwiSaver and the Super Fund; words match deeds.

text: The New Zealand Superannuation Fund is another excellent investment that we see. Sadly, it was paused under a previous National Government—they paused those Government contributions—and they were restarted again by the previous Labour Government.
explanation: Cites Labour’s record of restarting Super Fund contributions to back its long-term-planning claims—consistent words and deeds.

text: The principle is this: don't say anything that might attract a late night tweet from the White House. New Zealand's once proud, independent foreign policy has under this Government... been reduced to abject servility to the Trump White House.
explanation: Mocking characterisation ('abject servility') aimed at impugning the government rather than its policy reasoning.

text: That's what they love to do every time they give a speech on agriculture—to sing hymns to our farmers in worship of their wondrousness, and I certainly wouldn't want to compete with them on that.
explanation: Mocking caricature of how the National benches speak about farmers — directed at rhetorical style rather than personal character, but still a sneer rather than engagement.

text: I was staggered to hear the ACT Party member saying they’re not even going to support a bill that’s only about transparency and disclosure of modern slavery—slavery—in supply chains.
explanation: Characterises ACT's stance as indifference to slavery transparency, glossing over the efficacy and cost arguments McClure actually made — a mild misrepresentation.

text: This is a very important issue, and I would march in the street on this issue—but that’s probably not saying much, because I would march in the street on lots of different issues.
explanation: Light, good-humoured tone with no attack on others.

text: Speaking in the debate on the first reading of the Immigration (Enhanced Risk Management) Amendment Bill, I incorrectly asserted that Erica Stanford had attended a five countries immigration ministers meeting. I withdraw that statement.
explanation: Retracts a false claim about an opponent respectfully and without spin.

text: ordinary people are waking up to the fact that this Government is acting in the interests of its rich mates and some ideologs—and, in the case of New Zealand First, some conspiracy theory "cookers"—in not acting in the interests of all New Zealanders, the long-term interests, making sure the firefighters get the equipment they need to work. They're doing this because they don't understand, or they're beholden to donors.
explanation: Heavy personal/name-calling ('rich mates', 'ideologs', 'cookers', 'beholden to donors') rather than engaging the substance.

text: Yeah. It’s been out for years. What are you talking about? It’s like, update your negs, man. God, you’re so out of date.
explanation: Dismissive personal jab at an interjector rather than substantive engagement.

text: Let’s be honest about what this is about: this is about secrecy for the ultra-wealthy.
explanation: Imputes a covert, self-serving motive (protecting the rich) to the Government rather than engaging the substance of the section 17GB repeal.

text: We have an insane wish list of hyper-expensive, unfundable highways that the Government wants to pay for, and then, of course, local government has the real heavy lifting and responsibility to deliver public transport, walking, and cycling.
explanation: 'Insane wish list' is hyperbolic, though aimed at the policy/spending, not a person.

text: I thank the Minister for his contribution. I did want to ask a couple of questions of clarification about the numbers he just gave us.
explanation: Courteous, clarification-seeking opening focused on the figures.

text: the Green Party, who, if you look at their social media posts, would be quite happy for Kiwis to live in the dark, drive nothing, and maybe actually go back to a time when New Zealand was poor
explanation: A caricature of the Greens' positions amounting to a strawman attack.

text: what you Sim City obsessed planning nerds believe should be the right number of houses, Tamatha Paul
explanation: Direct name-calling (“planning nerds”) aimed at a named member.

text: They can choose to live out a SimCity planner’s unicorn world where there’s a 10-kilometre radius around the CBD and not a single house should ever be built outside it, or they can choose to listen to Aucklanders.
explanation: Mocking framing of opponents' position rather than engaging it.

text: So the member Tamatha Paul makes a good point: the Resource Management Act is broken.
explanation: Respectful acknowledgement of an opposing member's argument.

text: Now, Phil to some of us is a hero. I probably shouldn’t be admitting that as an ACT MP, but the National Policy Statement on Urban Development, Mr Twyford, actually set the scene for why it’s important to build up around these expensive investments in transport, like the City Rail Link
explanation: Respectful and gracious toward a political opponent.

text: Power bills are up 18 percent under National.
explanation: A precise partisan statistic; the figure and its attribution to 'under National' are contestable without sourcing.

text: the Super Fund had a little lesson in this recently when the High Court found that they had not actually met their mandated legislative obligations to ensure that the investment of New Zealand Superannuation Funds should not be in things like Israel’s illegal occupation of the Palestinian territories.
explanation: Asserts a specific High Court finding against the Super Fund; presented as fact but the precise holding is not verifiable from the text and may overstate the ruling's scope.

text: Xinjiang province, which produces about 20 percent of the world’s cotton consumption. Campaigners allege—the Chinese Government denies it, but campaigners allege and have produced evidence—that there are hundreds of thousands, if not more than a million, people engaged in State-imposed forced labour in Xinjiang province.
explanation: Xinjiang's ~20% share of world cotton and large-scale forced-labour allegations are well documented; he accurately attributes the claim to campaigners and notes the Chinese denial.

text: I was fascinated to read that our secondary legislation is published by a plethora of different agencies—central government and local government—and that estimates range from around 7,500 to 20,000 current instruments published by around 120 Government, local government, and non-Government agencies.
explanation: Factual claim about the scale and dispersion of secondary legislation; consistent with the bill's background material and plausibly accurate, though cited as an estimated range.

text: remember that under Labour's Helen Clark, New Zealand stayed out of the United States and the UK and Australia's disastrous invasion of Iraq in 2003
explanation: Accurate: NZ did not join the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

text: There is a way to clear the Strait of Hormuz and get the oil flowing again, and it's very simple. It's stop the war; stop the war.
explanation: 'Stop the war' is a slogan, not a mechanism NZ can deliver; no concrete steps offered.

text: Will you rule out sending New Zealand personnel and New Zealand defence assets to the Strait of Hormuz?
explanation: Targets a concrete, answerable commitment (ruling out personnel/assets to a named location).

text: Ken Roth, the former director of Human Rights Watch, is one of the international experts on this, and he was in New Zealand only days ago. He argues that due diligence should be the target, not just disclosure.
explanation: Names the expert and the precise policy distinction (due diligence vs disclosure) at stake at select committee.

text: now this law is going to place an obligation on all of the publishing agencies—the 120 different agencies will be obliged to actually publish the secondary legislation that they are responsible for, a number of other obligations, as well, in the way that that information is kept and published, and then PCO simply will provide internet links to all of those off that main website.
explanation: Describes the concrete mechanism of the bill: distributed publishing obligations on 120 agencies plus PCO linking, rather than vague praise.

text: Some 1,145 people did the survey from all across West Auckland, and when I asked people what the most important issue for them was, they overwhelmingly said cost of living—48 percent said cost of living.
explanation: Names sample size, location, and exact percentage.

text: There is a way to clear the Strait of Hormuz and get the oil flowing again, and it's very simple. It's stop the war; stop the war.
explanation: Identifies the root cause but presents an oversimplified single solution as 'very simple'.

text: the Super Fund had a little lesson in this recently when the High Court found that they had not actually met their mandated legislative obligations to ensure that the investment of New Zealand Superannuation Funds should not be in things like Israel’s illegal occupation of the Palestinian territories.
explanation: Uses a concrete legal precedent to support the social-licence argument, though the example's characterisation carries some argumentative spin.

text: It's always worth remembering, with regulation, that our recent history in this country is stuffed full of examples of badly judged regulation. We only need to look at, for instance, the building products, we only need to look at health and safety, where the balance has not been in the right place.
explanation: Supports the call for careful scrutiny with cited examples (building products, health and safety) where regulatory balance went wrong; reasoned, though the examples are named rather than detailed.

text: if you want to have the free flow of capital around the world, for goodness’ sake, do something about maintaining social licence for that, like actually protecting some basic ethical standards, which is what this bill does. If you don’t, you risk losing public confidence and public support in the very system that you want.
explanation: Coherent argument that ethical guardrails sustain the social licence free markets depend on; reasons from the opponents' own premises (free-market commitment).

text: Xinjiang province, which produces about 20 percent of the world’s cotton consumption. Campaigners allege—the Chinese Government denies it, but campaigners allege and have produced evidence—that there are hundreds of thousands, if not more than a million, people engaged in State-imposed forced labour in Xinjiang province.
explanation: Carefully distinguishes allegation from proven fact, names the counter-position, and grounds magnitude in cited evidence.

text: ordinary people are waking up to the fact that this Government is acting in the interests of its rich mates and some ideologs—and, in the case of New Zealand First, some conspiracy theory "cookers"—in not acting in the interests of all New Zealanders, the long-term interests, making sure the firefighters get the equipment they need to work. They're doing this because they don't understand, or they're beholden to donors.
explanation: Ad hominem and imputed motives ('beholden to donors', 'rich mates') asserted without evidence.

text: We have enough—we have enough wealth and resources in Aotearoa to end child poverty. We could do that. It’s a political decision not to do that.
explanation: A defensible framing (poverty as a distributional choice) but asserted without evidence on the actual fiscal cost or feasibility.

text: When you look overseas at cities that have really good outcomes, most of the power and the funding is devolved to the city to make the decision about transport priorities. It's not done at a national level.
explanation: Appeals to overseas examples to support devolution but names no specific cities or data.

text: if there is no specific requirement to think about disabled access then it will often get missed and it will be more expensive to remedy later.
explanation: Reasoned cause-and-effect drawn from experience with prior regional committee requirements.

text: how do we know it's delivering on these objectives, and what's the definition or measure that we're using to measure productivity?
explanation: Demands measurable definitions and a means of verification for the stated objectives — disciplined questioning.

text: so far, it’s pretty obvious that for a lot of people on the Government benches, you know, math is not their strong point; I’m being very diplomatic here. Not everybody is, you know, mathematically inclined in their reasoning, and it’s obvious that the members in the Government are not mathematically inclined.
explanation: Belittling, us-vs-them framing that alienates rather than persuades the people she's addressing.

text: Yeah. It’s been out for years. What are you talking about? It’s like, update your negs, man. God, you’re so out of date.
explanation: Combative put-down that shuts down dialogue.

text: I look forward to changing the Government later this year, to one that cares about our people.
explanation: Implies the current Government does not care about people; partisan rather than unifying.

text: Members opposite may claim to care about equality of opportunity, but unless they address the structural inequities in our economy through progressive taxation, then there is no equality of opportunity.
explanation: Casts opponents' stated values as empty; appeals to her own side rather than seeking common ground.

text: if there is no specific requirement to think about disabled access then it will often get missed and it will be more expensive to remedy later.
explanation: Advocates inclusively for disabled users' lived experience.

text: But, luckily, we have an election later this year and we can choose something much more sensible and long term.
explanation: Predicts an election later in 2026 — verifiable and consistent with NZ's fixed parliamentary term; the partisan editorialising aside, the core forecast is reliable.

text: It is true that we do not have enough petrol and diesel, and we are probably going to run out of diesel in the next few weeks.
explanation: Forecasts a national diesel shortage within a few weeks; specific and falsifiable but a strong, uncertain claim hedged with 'probably'.

text: I look forward to changing the Government later this year, to one that cares about our people.
explanation: Asked via the point of order to withdraw and apologise for imputing improper motives, she pivots entirely to a partisan talking point rather than addressing it.

text: it was, I think, a 0.2 percent growth in GDP over the entire last year
explanation: Selectively cites one quarter's figure as the whole year; Nancy Lu notes a 0.9% September quarter, so this understates measured growth.

text: when those were lowered, actually, the income tax rate collection rate went up in New Zealand.
explanation: Revenue did rise after the 1980s rate cuts, but attributing the rise to lower rates is contested (base-broadening and growth also mattered); directionally defensible, causally overstated.

text: they did this in March 2024—they removed the exemption for light electric vehicles and for plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. They have removed the exemption for road user charges. So they made it more expensive to own an EV.
explanation: Dated, specific policy claim (March 2024 RUC exemption removal) that matches the known record.

text: It has reversed the ban on offshore oil and gas. It has excluded agriculture from the emissions trading scheme (ETS). It has ended the Clean Car Discount. It has gotten rid of the Climate Emergency Response Fund. It has weakened climate reporting... It has cancelled Auckland light rail. It has added road-user charges to electric vehicles.
explanation: Most items (offshore oil/gas reversal, ending Clean Car Discount, agriculture out of ETS, cancelling Auckland light rail, RUCs on EVs) match the public record; framing of a few is contestable.

text: Labour—and thank you, Sir Michael Cullen—is the party that set up the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, that sovereign wealth fund that will enable us to stay prosperous into the future.
explanation: The NZ Super Fund was established under the Cullen-era Labour government; accurate.

text: All climate action is basically action on cost of living, particularly when we look at the rising cost of oil internationally, so it simply makes sense for New Zealand to become less reliant on imported fossil fuels for transport.
explanation: Reasonable directional claim about import exposure, but the universal framing overstates it.

text: When you look overseas at cities that have really good outcomes, most of the power and the funding is devolved to the city to make the decision about transport priorities. It's not done at a national level.
explanation: Broadly accurate that many high-performing cities have devolved transport powers, though stated as a sweeping generalisation.

text: We recently received answers from the Minister stating that about $200 million of funding was declined for towns right around the country—like New Plymouth and Dunedin, Wellington, Hawke’s Bay, Nelson—had funding declined for improved or expanded public transport services, which would probably really come in handy right now.
explanation: Attributes the figure to the Minister's own answers, making it relatively well-grounded.

text: I think 20 years ago, Sue Kedgley was announcing the Green Party policy of an ombudsman on supermarkets, and we saw some version of that finally get implemented.
explanation: Broadly accurate that the Greens long advocated supermarket oversight and a grocery commissioner was later created; the '20 years' and exact framing are approximate.

text: if you look at page 66 of this report, it shows that New Zealand, far from being a high-tax country, is a country where we’re collecting lower than the OECD average in terms of Government revenue as a percentage of GDP.
explanation: NZ's general-government revenue as a share of GDP is below the OECD average; consistent with the cited report.

text: The four-phase plan that we've seen, that's now in the public domain, is simple yet pragmatic, and it's so good, even the Australians are starting to copy it.
explanation: The claim that Australia is copying the plan is unsubstantiated and self-congratulatory.

text: some payments were made to people who were not intended to receive them, such as—wait for it, Sam Uffindell—people who were overseas; think French backpackers or, in some cases, deceased people.
explanation: Misdirected payments did occur in some COVID schemes, but the colourful 'French backpackers/deceased' framing is selective and rhetorical.

text: the International Monetary Fund and the OECD estimated the discretionary fiscal response was approximately 20 percent of GDP for our COVID response, and this is among the largest COVID-19 responses globally.
explanation: NZ's fiscal response was indeed among the larger ones; the ~20% figure is broadly defensible attributed to IMF/OECD.

text: The average hospital is 45 years old. Education: one-third of our school buildings are more than 50 years old and nearly half are between 20 and 15 years old, many with deferred maintenance.
explanation: Asset-age statistics consistent with infrastructure reporting, though the '20 and 15 years' phrasing is garbled.

text: As at 30 June 2024, the Crown held $571 billion in assets, or roughly $107,000 per person, and $380 billion in liabilities. This leaves a net worth of $191 billion
explanation: Reports Crown balance-sheet figures consistent with the investment statement being debated.

text: We have a plan for action on the cost of living. We have a plan for good jobs at home that pay enough to get ahead. We have a plan for healthcare that you can actually afford and for homes that do not take up all your income.
explanation: Repeated 'we have a plan' with no detail on mechanisms, figures, or timeframes — vague platitudes.

text: Twenty thousand New Zealanders are still alive, the lowest excess mortality rate in the world—businesses have survived; livelihoods that were protected. That’s what we have to show for it.
explanation: Gives a figure and a named metric but the claim of lives saved is broad.

text: The Parliamentary Commissioner of the Environment—a former National Party MP, and a man who was appointed to the role by Labour and reappointed by National—said, “For these reasons, the Ministry for the Environment should, in my view, be left out of this merger.”
explanation: Identifies the official, his background, and quotes his recommendation.

text: They've come across clients who have four or five or six or seven or eight buy now, pay later loans; they get rid of one only to get another and they build up and up and up. Not just that, but they have people who are using buy now, pay later for everyday consumable items: food and petrol... So I do think we need some more regulation in the buy now, pay later space, particularly when it comes to vulnerable borrowers.
explanation: Concrete detail — clients stacking up to eight BNPL loans, use for consumables like food and petrol — leading to a defined policy ask on BNPL regulation.

text: A person can enter into a credit contract to buy a car, but then the lender can, if the repayments on that car are not being met, install a disabling device; a tyre lock on the car. And, in fact, you have to pay an upfront cost that's included in the fee for installing that device; you have to pay a regular rental payment for the device to be active, and then there's a fee for removing the device at the end of the loan.
explanation: Highly concrete: describes the exact mechanism (disabling device/tyre lock) and the three distinct fees (install, rental, removal) layered onto borrowers.

text: We have enough—we have enough wealth and resources in Aotearoa to end child poverty. We could do that. It’s a political decision not to do that.
explanation: States a goal (end child poverty) but no mechanism, figures, or named policy for how.

text: this Government needs to grapple with the reality that the Roads of National Significance it campaigned on are unfundable and not the best use of money.
explanation: Names a specific programme but asserts 'unfundable' without supporting figures here.

text: if there is no specific requirement to think about disabled access then it will often get missed and it will be more expensive to remedy later.
explanation: Refers to a past legislative requirement but no figures or named mechanism for the current bill.

text: the way the current Government policy statement (GPS) is set up, it sets aside the largest share of funding that’s going on new infrastructure or new projects just to be on State highways, and the vast majority of the public transport services and infrastructure budget is to maintain existing services, not to increase services.
explanation: Describes the funding allocation structure concretely though without dollar figures.

text: We recently received answers from the Minister stating that about $200 million of funding was declined for towns right around the country—like New Plymouth and Dunedin, Wellington, Hawke’s Bay, Nelson—had funding declined for improved or expanded public transport services, which would probably really come in handy right now.
explanation: Cites a ~$200m figure and names the towns affected, sourced to ministerial answers.

text: This came out of a review that was led by the Minister for Regulation, the Minister for Primary Industries, the Ministry for the Environment, the Environmental Protection Agency—it's a no brainer. I commend the bill to the House.
explanation: Names the bodies behind the review but says nothing concrete about what the bill changes.

text: For a small country that feeds 40 million people, it's pretty crucial.
explanation: Offers one concrete figure but no further detail about the policy mechanism.

text: some payments were made to people who were not intended to receive them, such as—wait for it, Sam Uffindell—people who were overseas; think French backpackers or, in some cases, deceased people.
explanation: Gives concrete categories of erroneous recipients.

text: the large asset programme, or the LSAP, as it’s more affectionately known, has shown losses of $10.5 billion as early as last year—$10.5 billion.
explanation: Names the programme and a precise loss figure.

text: As at 30 June 2024, the Crown held $571 billion in assets, or roughly $107,000 per person, and $380 billion in liabilities. This leaves a net worth of $191 billion
explanation: Precise dated figures including a per-person breakdown.

text: That was what David Seymour spent his time on, and that shows why the ACT Party is losing in the polls at the moment.
explanation: Non sequitur — a speech topic does not establish the cause of polling movements.

text: The more little special rules that are sitting there, the easier it is for people to circumvent the intent of the tax system.
explanation: Reasonable causal argument (more carve-outs leads to more avoidance opportunities), but asserted as a principle without supporting evidence.

text: This Government needs to remember that business is a subset of the environment, not the other way around. Business is a subset of the economy. It is a subset of the environment—the economy is a subset of the environment. We cannot work in business unless we have a livable world.
explanation: A coherent nested-dependency argument (economy depends on environment), though presented as axiom rather than evidenced.

text: The Parliamentary Commissioner of the Environment—a former National Party MP, and a man who was appointed to the role by Labour and reappointed by National—said, “For these reasons, the Ministry for the Environment should, in my view, be left out of this merger.”
explanation: Marshals a cross-party authority (appointed by both major parties) to lend weight to the conclusion.

text: We know that the Inland Revenue Department hasn't collected the data yet, because the income tax year hasn't ended, so there is no data available from the Inland Revenue Department. On what grounds can the Minister say that that policy is a success
explanation: Evidence-focused challenge: success claims require data, and she explains why no data can yet exist (tax year not ended).

text: In fact, many of those projects—50 percent of those projects—didn’t even start until two years after the funding was approved, so they can hardly be called shovel-ready.
explanation: Draws a labelled conclusion ('hardly shovel-ready') from a cited statistic about start times.

text: a bit more than half of that increase, $119 billion, was not new capability; it was re-evaluations driven by inflation; rising land and construction costs, especially for State highways, rail, and public buildings. This means our balance sheet looks stronger on paper without delivering more or better services.
explanation: Distinguishes paper revaluation from real capability — a sound analytical point with a figure attached.

text: But you know why they're not signing it? Do you know why they're politicking in the midst of a campaign year? Because they're jealous. Because they didn't do it.
explanation: Pure speculation about motive ('jealous') offered as explanation with no evidence.

text: This bill is really quite simple. It’s about taking the environment ministry and putting it into another ministry. Nothing’s disappearing. There’s no drama. Cheer up; the sun is shining. I commend the bill to the House.
explanation: Minimises the change ('nothing's disappearing') by assertion, dismissing the substantive concerns raised without engaging them.

text: This came out of a review that was led by the Minister for Regulation, the Minister for Primary Industries, the Ministry for the Environment, the Environmental Protection Agency—it's a no brainer. I commend the bill to the House.
explanation: Leans on the authority of who led the review and the dismissive 'it's a no brainer' rather than presenting the bill's actual merits or evidence.

text: Labour is the party that introduced KiwiSaver, that has enabled New Zealanders to build their own savings for retirement.
explanation: Claim of being a long-term-planning party is backed by an actual delivered policy on her own record — words match deeds.

text: It was deeply inconvenient to us as a Government at the time, but I'm looking at it now and thinking, actually, it's really worth looking at.
explanation: Candid admission that her own former government found the 2022 IR briefing inconvenient; self-aware rather than self-serving, a consistent-with-record acknowledgement.

text: In response to that crisis, when we saved 20,000 lives in New Zealand, when we saved businesses, and when we saved jobs, they say we got it wrong.
explanation: Defends her own government's record consistently with Labour's prior position on the COVID response.

text: We had KiwiSaver set up by a Labour Government and the New Zealand Super Fund set up by a Labour Government.
explanation: Backs the claim of long-term planning with two real, delivered institutions on Labour's record.

text: My question is: in Budget 2024, the actual proof is that we saw a lot of cuts to front-line services, so does the Minister stand by her statement that there will be no cuts to front-line services?
explanation: Frames the attack as the Minister's words (no cuts) clashing with her actions (cuts) — a hypocrisy charge about the opponent, not the speaker.

text: Does she stand by her statement that "This Government has got your back." when 70 percent of workers didn't get a pay rise above inflation in the last year?
explanation: Targets a perceived gap between the Government's 'got your back' slogan and worker outcomes—an authenticity challenge to the opponent, not a self-signal.

text: Labour is the party that introduced KiwiSaver, that has enabled New Zealanders to build their own savings for retirement.
explanation: Names a concrete policy Labour designed and implemented, not merely promised.

text: Labour—and thank you, Sir Michael Cullen—is the party that set up the New Zealand Superannuation Fund, that sovereign wealth fund that will enable us to stay prosperous into the future.
explanation: Credits Labour with a concrete, delivered institution still operating today.

text: We have promised a Future Fund for a future made in New Zealand.
explanation: A promise/announcement with no delivery demonstrated.

text: We had KiwiSaver set up by a Labour Government and the New Zealand Super Fund set up by a Labour Government.
explanation: Points to concrete, enduring policies actually delivered rather than promised.

text: We set up the national resilience plan, which then the National Party scrapped as one of their first decisions coming into Government in 2023.
explanation: Claims delivery of a plan, but undercut by its being scrapped — follow-through did not endure.

text: The Minister of Finance is a failure, and this Budget Policy Statement just reinforces that.
explanation: Blunt personal verdict ('is a failure') on the Minister rather than her policies.

text: That was what David Seymour spent his time on, and that shows why the ACT Party is losing in the polls at the moment.
explanation: Turns a critique of Seymour's speech into a jab about his party's polling rather than the substance.

text: I think we need a little bit of humility from that side about what might or might not affect New Zealand.
explanation: Pointed but mild rebuke about consistency; aimed at conduct/argument, not personal abuse.

text: We know that the Inland Revenue Department hasn't collected the data yet, because the income tax year hasn't ended, so there is no data available from the Inland Revenue Department. On what grounds can the Minister say that that policy is a success
explanation: Demands evidence and engages the claim's basis rather than attacking the Minister personally.

text: While we've tidied up some stuff like the mobile truck-lending that was going on—and I'd like to pay credit, in particular, to Andrew Bayly, who was very strong on this and talked about how he had chased those trucks out of his electorate every time he saw them; frankly, I'm with Mr Bayly on that.
explanation: Warm, respectful acknowledgement of an opponent's good work; the model of policy-focused, person-respecting debate.

text: We are truly living in the Upside Down, where we have a Minister of the Government saying ... something that is so demonstrably untrue.
explanation: Accuses the Minister of stating something 'demonstrably untrue' — pointed, edging toward an integrity attack though tied to the bill text.

text: none of this is actually logical; it is ideological.
explanation: Dismissive of the Government's motives but framed as a critique of reasoning rather than a personal insult.

text: Is that why they're striking twice a week?
explanation: Pointed interjection challenging the Government's record, focused on the policy outcome rather than personal insult.

text: Can the Minister of Finance clearly articulate for us how exactly this Government has apparently increased our resilience while actively subsidising new fossil-fuel production and cutting investment in renewable energy generation?
explanation: Sharp framing ('apparently') but a substantive challenge on the resilience-vs-fossil-fuel contradiction.

text: Why did his Government decide to cut flood protection funding at a time when extreme weather is becoming more frequent and severe, by approximately half compared to the former Government?
explanation: Pointed but substantive — challenges a budget decision on policy grounds without personal attack.

text: Do you know anything about transparency, Mr O’Connor?
explanation: A direct personal jibe at a named member rather than substantive debate.

text: So in the midst of challenging times in New Zealand, I'm pleased to report that the adults are in the room and this Government will steer New Zealand through these rocky waters.
explanation: 'The adults are in the room' implies opponents are childish/incompetent — a disparaging contrast.

text: we saw the COVID royal commission inquiry and we saw $60 billion wasted, half of that and not even associated with the direct response of COVID; shovel-ready projects that were nowhere near a shovel, lump-sum payments to dead people.
explanation: Mocking characterisation ('nowhere near a shovel') of the previous government's programmes.

text: some payments were made to people who were not intended to receive them, such as—wait for it, Sam Uffindell—people who were overseas; think French backpackers or, in some cases, deceased people.
explanation: Uses a vivid, slightly mocking example ('wait for it') though aimed at programme design rather than a person.

text: I’d like to congratulate the other member there, Georgie Dansey, on what I assume is her first 10-minute call. Well done, you’ve completed the challenge.
explanation: Warm cross-party congratulation to a Labour member; collegial.

text: In the 1960s, there were seven New Zealanders aged 15 to 64 for every New Zealander over the age of 65. Now, it is the case that it is one in four, and in 2065 it will be one in two.
explanation: The 2065 ratio is a long-range demographic forecast, well-grounded in current projections but inherently uncertain.

text: I think it’s a real problem, when you open this long-term fiscal statement, that you see that debt will reach 200 percent of GDP. At the moment, it’s in the low 40s.
explanation: A 40-year debt forecast; he himself notes it won't materialise, so it's a conditional projection of high uncertainty.

text: where there were, only a few decades ago, 15 taxpayers or working people for every retiree; there’s now only four. In a couple of decades, there will only be two people of working age—and that’s defined as 15 to 64—for every person over 65.
explanation: Projects a 2-to-1 ratio in two decades, consistent with demographic forecasts.

text: I think it is important to have some semblance of respect in this House towards each other. Every member is supposed to be an honourable member.
explanation: Appeals to shared norms across the House, though prompted by a personal grievance.

text: …if she really wants us to be as rich as Australia, I suggest that she supports the Resource Management Act reforms and she also supports fast track and she supports mining. If she does that, we will be richer than Australia.
explanation: Partisan challenge to an opponent rather than persuasion or common ground.

text: Some of them we can make together. For some of them, quite clearly our values won’t align.
explanation: Acknowledges scope for cross-party cooperation while being honest about differences — a measured, bridge-leaving tone.

text: I do want to acknowledge the Finance and Expenditure Committee's work on this. We had very constructive discussions around whether some of the measures went far enough... I do want to also acknowledge the 275 individuals and groups who submitted on this bill.
explanation: Inclusive, bridge-building tone that credits collaborative process.

text: He is the leader of our country and has been remarkably missing from this fuel crisis. At a time when we have care and support workers who cannot afford to go to their jobs... where is the Prime Minister?
explanation: Effective rhetorical hook (the 'Where's Wally' frame) but purely combative, appealing to her own side.

text: how does this temporary brief oversight for a few minutes compare with the over $52 million bribe through the Public Interest Journalism Fund?
explanation: Characterising the PIJF as a 'bribe' contingent on running 'a certain narrative' is a misleading mischaracterisation of the fund.

text: How does the Government reconcile signing on to the India free-trade agreement’s novel immigration settings for 5,000 new migrant visas covering “skills shortages” like musicians and yoga teachers when there are 163,000 unemployed New Zealanders?
explanation: The ~163,000 unemployed figure is roughly plausible, but characterising the 5,000 visas as 'musicians and yoga teachers' is misleading — Stanford shows most are green-list roles.

text: We have for decades stood up for freedom of navigation in the Middle East and through the Indo-Pacific.
explanation: Accurate as a general characterisation of NZ's long-held support for freedom of navigation.

text: This one we don’t quite understand, because, unlike Australia, New Zealand has not expressed explicit support for the US attacks on Iran. Instead, we acknowledged those US attacks and said we understood the reasons behind them, without ourselves endorsing them.
explanation: Draws a precise factual distinction between NZ's 'acknowledged/understood' framing and Australia's explicit support; presented carefully and plausibly accurate.

text: The questioner, in his question, insinuated that a foreigner without any status in this country nevertheless could make financial contributions to political parties. That statement is false. It's outside the law, and he's been here long enough to have learnt that.
explanation: New Zealand law restricts overseas/anonymous donations, so the assertion that foreign nationals without status cannot lawfully donate is broadly correct.

text: They lament that the New Zealand Government does not currently place an emphasis on mindless moral posturing and vacuous virtue signalling. You get that? We will never do that. Our focus is on dealing with the world as it is, not as we would wish it to be, and on getting the best possible outcomes for New Zealanders.
explanation: 'Dealing with the world as it is' is a slogan with no concrete policy content.

text: If we receive a request or if an international coalition was established in the future to safeguard commercial shipping, any possible contribution will be a matter for—guess who!—the Cabinet, first of all, to determine, based on careful consideration of New Zealand’s interests. That’s what we intend to do.
explanation: Specifies the conditional and the decision process (Cabinet, on NZ's interests), though no concrete commitment.

text: New Zealand is not taking part in the conflict and does not intend to. New Zealand supports de-escalation, an end to this conflict, and the restoration of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
explanation: States a concrete NZ position (non-participation, de-escalation, freedom of navigation in a named strait) though without mechanisms or actions.

text: Over the weekend, New Zealand joined a statement with 21 other countries, emphasising the importance of getting ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz so that fuel and goods can be transported freely.
explanation: Names the timeframe, the number of countries (21 others), and the subject of the statement.

text: Why sign an FTA which included the phrase, "nothing in this Agreement shall preclude the adoption by New Zealand of measures it deems necessary to accord more favourable treatment to Māori", given that this language runs counter to the coalition Government's approach that all New Zealanders should be equal under the law?
explanation: Quotes the exact clause and ties it to a stated principle.

text: That account is dedicated to a range of expenses, and if the member would like to write me a letter without squiggles, I shall provide a detailed answer.
explanation: Asked a precise figure (the levy account balance) and refuses to give one, deflecting with a quip.

text: Far be it for to add to such tawdry discussions. This is a serious issue where Kiwis are deeply concerned about the cost of living, the security of fuel, and options going forward. It really doesn't uphold the status of the House—that tawdry contribution.
explanation: Asked whether he's deflecting to cover his own failure; doesn't engage the substance, dismisses the question as 'tawdry'.

text: Ah, yes. I have sought advice on this issue and I have been advised that the 960 million litres worth of fuel we may have access to by dint of international options was paid for by money in a levy account. That money has been well spent, and, of course, it could not have been spent on an imaginary, non-existent dream.
explanation: Concedes 'yes' he sought advice but reframes the answer around international options rather than the specific surplus-funded reserve asked about.

text: I have taken the liberty of speaking to the CEO of Port Taranaki, one of the entities that was involved with what the Hon Megan Woods is referring to. Sadly, that CEO has confirmed to me that such a proposal could never work because of the regulatory unwillingness of the last Government to make it easier for such a thing to be developed, and the only reason that the member is talking about 70 million litres of storage is because she closed 700 million litres down.
explanation: Engages the diesel-reserve question but routes it back into blame.

text: I have also been advised that, globally, we consume 100 million barrels of crude oil per day. Twenty million barrels was previously going through the strait; 2.6 million barrels of that volume came from Kuwait, and less than 10 percent of that crude oil makes its way to South-east Asia.
explanation: Directly addresses the advice he has seen on the Kuwait force-majeure impact on supply.

text: On behalf of the Prime Minister, I would say to Billy Clemens: be very careful how people may use your quotes for political advantage in Parliament.
explanation: Entirely dodges the substantive freight-vulnerability concern, addressing the quoted person instead.

text: Just in the last few hours, it has announced that those who face the greatest and most acute challenges with the cost of living are going to get an extra $50 a week to help absorb the pressure of this crisis, and we’re doing it in a way that is targeted, that is temporary, and that is timely.
explanation: Pivots from Verrall's questions about home-care workers and prescription fees to the new package, partially addressing cost-of-living but not the specific points.

text: I absolutely have confidence in the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries because he has listened to feedback and changed course. He’s listened to what people out there are saying and actually adapted his course to do the right thing.
explanation: Directly affirms confidence and gives a reason (the Minister changed course on the reforms).

text: The number one factor is that we need to ensure that Government behaviour does not add to inflation... we wanted to help people who are in the greatest need so we said that this is for people who are on the lower end of the income scale and who have children and who work... and we linked it to petrol prices so that if petrol prices come back down, we stop spending the money.
explanation: Directly answers what factors the Government weighed.

text: Yes. For a long time, there was, really, a blind eye being turned to the possibility of prosecution, there having been none for six years. In the last year, 34 different students have been referred to the Ministry of Education for prosecution. Of those, 17 have decided they would rather go back to attending school.
explanation: Asked whether the threat of prosecution has been effective; answers 'yes' and supplies supporting figures.

text: That question is totally illogical. It comes to a conclusion without any evidence whatsoever, and so I’m not wasting my time answering it.
explanation: Explicitly refuses to answer Tuiono's question about the legality of the strikes.

text: Because the job I am entrusted with is the Minister of Foreign Affairs of New Zealand, not the professor of international law at Woketown University, we take judicious, prudent decisions based on the national interest rather than offering empty virtue signalling.
explanation: Responds to a point of order about whether the PM directed him with rhetoric, not an answer.

text: The reality was that I was offshore, late at night, and got an enquiry, and we just sent back, in an abbreviated text, how it would possibly look and part of our discussion, and then went straight back to the original decision we made. That’s how we landed on that.
explanation: Asked whether he stands by his office's 'imprudent' description; explains the context but never directly affirms or retracts the description.

text: If we receive a request or if an international coalition was established in the future to safeguard commercial shipping, any possible contribution will be a matter for—guess who!—the Cabinet, first of all, to determine, based on careful consideration of New Zealand’s interests. That’s what we intend to do.
explanation: Directly addresses the central charge (that NZ is committing forces) by stating any contribution would require a future Cabinet decision.

text: The Minister of Foreign Affairs is charged with that responsibility but in consultation with the Prime Minister, obviously; the ministerial contacts, as well; and other MPs, including sometimes crossing the House to make sure that there is a unified view in this country.
explanation: Directly answers who the final decision-maker is (the Foreign Minister, in consultation).

text: Oh, well, in the interests of making democracy efficient, I apologise if I’ve upset the tender mercies of Taranaki.
explanation: Withdraws under pressure but the mocking tone undercuts the sincerity of the apology.

text: Sadly, life is not static. I can confirm, however, that there a host of areas in New Zealand where it would be very inappropriate to mine. Whether or not those places will be permanently off limits, obviously, waits for a future regime.
explanation: Responding to his own 2010 anti-mining quote, he concedes a shift ('life is not static') — an acknowledged change of position.

text: I can provide no better answer than to go to the Good Book: "When I was a child, I thought as a child."
explanation: Dismisses his earlier anti-mining views as childish — an open repudiation of a prior position, i.e. a flip.

text: We have for decades stood up for freedom of navigation in the Middle East and through the Indo-Pacific.
explanation: Frames the current stance as consistent with a long-standing, bipartisan NZ position on freedom of navigation; broadly defensible.

text: The Government's intention has always been to support industry members as they transition away from greyhound racing. … The bill allows for support, and the transition agency has flexibility to provide for additional compensation, such as for lost income, should this be seen as necessary.
explanation: Claims consistency between stated intent and the bill's provisions, pointing to mechanisms already in the law.

text: We have a habit of when we make a mistake, we admit it. We don’t think that we’re perfect... In this case, I made an assumption, and I should have had it checked out, and that’s the reason why we’re updating our systems at the moment.
explanation: Owns the error rather than deflecting; words match the admission of fault.

text: this is a great bill, which I am very proud to be commending to the House.
explanation: Vague praise ('a great bill') with no substantive detail about what the bill does or why.

text: The Reserve Bank said, last October, that during the pandemic, aggressive fiscal and monetary support helped avert deeper harm, but that the combined responses ultimately contributed to an inflation outbreak.
explanation: Attributes the claim to a named body and timeframe.

text: Treasury’s long-term insights briefing, highlighted by the finance Minister last August, examined the way the Government finances were used during and after the COVID period and said that the responses wound up costing NZ$66 billion
explanation: Names the source, the figure, and the timing.

text: temporary, targeted, and timely support for 143,000 of the working families with children, to support them through this very tough time, through the in-work tax credit.
explanation: Names the mechanism (in-work tax credit), the cohort, and a figure (143,000).

text: the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, who mentioned only just one quarter of the growth—very, very selective in her speech, that she failed to mentioned the 0.9 percent growth in the September 2025 quarter, then followed by another positive-growth quarter of 0.2 percent in the December quarter. Together, that is 1.1 percent growth in the last half year
explanation: Exact quarterly growth figures with named quarters.

text: I want to acknowledge those that were involved in building the straight track at the Wanganui Racecourse for its positive impact on the health of greyhounds since that has been opened.
explanation: Asserts a positive welfare impact from the straight track; plausible and specific but offered without evidence and hard to verify.

text: I cannot sit here and not note that it is my colleague Greg Fleming, a member of the National-led Government, the National Party, that has actually got this to the House during our Government. Labour had the opportunity in 2021; they didn’t get it there, so well done Greg and well done to Camilla.
explanation: Claim that Labour had the chance in 2021 and didn't deliver is plausible and consistent with the bill's history, though no specifics are given.

text: Where's there's not an appropriate product approved for a dog or a cat, we use the equivalent human medicine. These are available internationally, but they're not used here because we haven't been able to get them approved. This bill will enable us to use the right products for the right animals here in New Zealand.
explanation: Reflects the genuine off-label/unavailability issue in NZ veterinary medicine where human equivalents are substituted; broadly accurate drawing on his industry background.

text: I wanted to particularly thank all the members on the Finance and Expenditure Committee, including all the parties that have provided a lot of very valuable feedback, as well as the submitters who came before us and gave us real-life examples.
explanation: Wholly respectful acknowledgement of colleagues and contributors; no attack or sensationalism.

text: absolutely no to the spending, spending, spending on reckless projects like the last Government.
explanation: Critique of the previous government's fiscal approach; partisan and repetitive but policy-directed.

text: the Hon Dr Deborah Russell, who mentioned only just one quarter of the growth—very, very selective in her speech, that she failed to mentioned the 0.9 percent growth in the September 2025 quarter, then followed by another positive-growth quarter of 0.2 percent in the December quarter. Together, that is 1.1 percent growth in the last half year
explanation: Accuses an opponent of being 'very selective' but backs it with data rather than abuse.

text: I just want to take the opportunity to acknowledge the trainers, the industry players, and, particularly, those from Whanganui who are affected by the closure of this industry.
