text: This Government has taken us back 60 years—60 years.
explanation: Hyperbolic condemnation rather than substantive critique.

text: It starts a culture war, because that is exactly what the playbook of Trumpism does.
explanation: Associates opponents with a polarising foreign figure to delegitimise them.

text: this Government and this Minister continue to allow a persistent six-year life expectancy gap between Māori and non-Māori. That is a statistical fact that the Minister should be able to respond to
explanation: Holds the Minister accountable on substance ('continue to allow') without personal insult.

text: It should not be the excuse for “either/or”. We should surely be at the stage where we can “and, and”, and what we’ve seen is an erosion of another layer of protection of our taiao.
explanation: Critical but engages the framing of the issue, not persons.

text: It opens up the door for corporate exploiters. It makes sure there are no winners here. The only winners are those investors who this Government is well reputed for protecting. The loser here is the taiao. We do not support what the Government is intending to do with this bill. Shame on you.
explanation: Imputes corrupt motive ('protecting investors', 'corporate exploiters') and ends with 'Shame on you'—accusatory.

text: that Labour Government that was hopeless and that had overcooked the stimulus and driven up $100 billion of extra debt, driven up inflation, including 30 percent house price inflation in one year
explanation: 'Hopeless' is a character label rather than substantive critique, though it sits among policy claims.

text: we had a rise in crime, mainly driven by their culture of excuses—it wasn't your fault if you bashed somebody over the head; it was society's fault.
explanation: Caricatures opponents' views — deliberate misrepresentation.

text: I think it's 877, according to Copilot. We're nearly up to three years in Government.

text: There will be taxing the feijoas that fall off your tree, because they're so desperate.

text: We've got 199 days to get them out. We have the power, whānau. We have the ability to do that. Take it seriously, take people with you, and get them out now.

text: It should not be the excuse for “either/or”. We should surely be at the stage where we can “and, and”, and what we’ve seen is an erosion of another layer of protection of our taiao.
explanation: Reframes the debate inclusively ('and, and' rather than 'either/or'), inviting a both-ways approach.

text: There are two things that I believe this Parliament should always be united on. One is national security and the other one is emergency management.

text: Camilla Belich, who just spoke, who in my view has been an outstanding Opposition spokesperson for emergency management, and she has recently been promoted into the justice spokesperson role. You've been outstanding working with me.

text: We've got 199 days to get them out. We have the power, whānau. We have the ability to do that. Take it seriously, take people with you, and get them out now.

text: this Government and this Minister continue to allow a persistent six-year life expectancy gap between Māori and non-Māori. That is a statistical fact that the Minister should be able to respond to
explanation: Quantifies the gap but is broad on causes/solutions.

text: does the Minister accept the quoting of 80 percent renewable electricity masks the reality that less than half of our total energy use is actually renewable, and why is the Government relying on statistics that exclude industries such as transport?
explanation: Cites the 80%/half figures and names transport as the excluded sector.

text: Most will know that I’ve been part of the seabed mining kaupapa and the opposition to what we don’t want to happen in our environment—for 15 years in fact—and when you get down to the crux of it, when you get down to winning in the High Court, to winning in the Court of Appeal, to winning in the Supreme Court, they all came down to the role of what iwi and Te Tiriti had in that aspect.

text: Māori miss their first specialist appointments at 15.2 percent, compared to 4.7 percent for non-Māori. ... ambulatory sensitive hospitalisation (ASH) rates for tamariki Māori aged zero to four are at 8,510 per 100,000, versus 5,400 for non-Māori.

text: food prices are up around 9 percent since this Government took office.

text: This Government has taken us back 60 years—60 years.

text: does the Minister accept the quoting of 80 percent renewable electricity masks the reality that less than half of our total energy use is actually renewable, and why is the Government relying on statistics that exclude industries such as transport?
explanation: It is broadly accurate that headline renewable-electricity figures exclude transport and total energy.

text: Most will know that I’ve been part of the seabed mining kaupapa and the opposition to what we don’t want to happen in our environment—for 15 years in fact—and when you get down to the crux of it, when you get down to winning in the High Court, to winning in the Court of Appeal, to winning in the Supreme Court, they all came down to the role of what iwi and Te Tiriti had in that aspect.
explanation: The seabed-mining litigation (Trans-Tasman Resources) did turn substantially on tikanga and Treaty considerations through to the Supreme Court.

text: this Government and this Minister continue to allow a persistent six-year life expectancy gap between Māori and non-Māori. That is a statistical fact that the Minister should be able to respond to
explanation: The roughly six-year Māori/non-Māori life expectancy gap is well documented and the Minister effectively confirms it.

text: It starts a culture war, because that is exactly what the playbook of Trumpism does.
explanation: Reasons by analogy to 'Trumpism' rather than from evidence about the NZ policy itself.

text: does the Minister accept the quoting of 80 percent renewable electricity masks the reality that less than half of our total energy use is actually renewable, and why is the Government relying on statistics that exclude industries such as transport?
explanation: Draws a valid distinction between renewable electricity share and total energy use, a substantive analytical point.

text: if kaupapa Māori models were actually delivering results, why has the Government not mandated more investment towards taking these approaches to address this pile of poor statistics
explanation: Conditional argument linking effective models to the case for more investment, though it assumes the premise it asserts.

text: It opens up the door for corporate exploiters. It makes sure there are no winners here. The only winners are those investors who this Government is well reputed for protecting. The loser here is the taiao. We do not support what the Government is intending to do with this bill. Shame on you.
explanation: Attributes motive and predicts outcomes without supporting evidence in the passage.

text: Which targets have the milestone for the year under review been met and which have or will be met in the current financial year?

text: Which targets have the milestone for the year under review been met and which have or will be met in the current financial year?

text: I'd first like to open my address by acknowledging the amazing work, in very difficult circumstances, that our corrections officers do on a daily basis.

text: Regarding Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the bill fails to recognise that the Crown must take positive steps to protect Māori, and it does not meet the Crown's obligation of active protection.

text: I'd also like to acknowledge my colleague Camilla Belich's approach in this legislation.
explanation: Reaches across the aisle to credit an opposition member's approach — consensus-building rather than combative.

text: I’m old enough to know when we first introduced health and safety legislation and we fundamentally started with a reporting mechanism and a policy development. Over time, that legislation grew teeth, it grew strength, and it grew, most importantly, accountability for those who do wrong.

text: I do acknowledge the ACT member for talking about being judged by the outcomes of our legislation, and not just that we have legislation, but I think it has been traversed clearly in this House that this is the starting point that we need.

text: at its core, New Zealand First supports this bill because it is firmly rooted in our foundational belief that we need to protect community and country.

text: The bill makes additional amendments to the Corrections Act 2004, which was recently amended in 2025 to remove explicit references to Te Tiriti.

text: Māori make up a disproportionate amount of prisoners in the current prison system.

text: Would he not consider then, if those objectives are going to be imposed on Aucklanders, the insertion of a new subsection (3)(aa) that would read "reducing congestion" as one of the objectives of that plan, given that most Aucklanders tell pollsters and local politicians alike that congestion is their number one problem in Auckland's transport system

text: Regarding Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the bill fails to recognise that the Crown must take positive steps to protect Māori, and it does not meet the Crown's obligation of active protection.

text: I'll refer him to Land Transport (Road User) Rule 2004, which is the rule which most of these bylaws and other rules are made under, that confers ministerial power to set rules by regulation, and then local authorities are the bodies which are delegated to, within that, to make the rules.

text: the use of the new powers proposed under this bill is likely to have a disproportionate effect on Māori within the prison system and their whānau on the outside, who may also be subject to what are otherwise internal decisions made by managers from within prisons.

text: of course we know that in Corrections, when resources are strained, as they very much are at the current time, aspirations are rarely achieved.

text: Is it now the coalition Government's policy to override the recommendations from the Overseas Investment Office when assessing the benefit to New Zealand test and open the door to the sell-off of New Zealand farms to foreigners?

text: It's going bankrupt the country for the price of a Mount Vic extra tunnel. It's crazy, what's happening with this Government, fixated on their roads.

text: what concerns me with this bill, with its focus on Auckland—creates a bespoke solution for Auckland Transport—is that, actually, we'll see more and more funding going to Auckland and the transport system in Auckland, and therefore other cities across New Zealand will miss out on that needed funding.
explanation: Reasonable concern but the link from governance change to funding diversion is asserted, not demonstrated.

text: Last week, Retail NZ released a report … It said that an illicit tobacco market already existed and is only going to grow. … It also reduces revenue collection used to fund Government services, and … it allows organised crime groups to line their pockets and expand their reach in our communities.

text: While I was on the Transport and Infrastructure Committee and I generally support the direction, I just wanted to tease out some of what I would say were apparent inconsistencies.

text: they're not thrown out just because it was the other side that started them.

text: Why is it necessary, then, for the Government to have such a level of central planning as to impose on Aucklanders the three objectives there?

text: Until now, India had a 50 percent tariff on imported apples; under the FTA, New Zealand apples get that cut to 25 percent within a quota, and over time that will come down.

text: I'm totally distracted by that previous contribution and the load of waffle that we've just heard about electricity and electrification from the very people that were in Government when they wrecked the electricity sector in this country.
explanation: Dismisses the prior speech as 'waffle' and accuses opponents of having 'wrecked' the sector — dismissive and accusatory rather than substantive.

text: Some people said it couldn't be done; some people said it couldn't be done in the time frame. But what have we done? We've secured the FTA with India.

text: We've already announced three free doctors visits, free cervical cancer screening, a plan to get easier doctor appointments, and the Future Fund, which builds your future here in New Zealand.

text: By golly, in Nelson—a seat that we're going to take off Labour at the next election because of a hard-working MP who cares about them
explanation: An electoral prediction about winning Nelson; falsifiable but partisan optimism with no polling cited, so uncertain.

text: Until now, our wines have faced a staggering 150 percent tariff at the Indian border. Thanks to this agreement, those tariffs will drop to as low as 25 percent for many New Zealand wines
explanation: Names exact before/after tariff rates and the product category.

text: cherries will fall from 33 percent tariff to zero over time, which means more money for orchardists, more opportunities for seasonal workers, and a real incentive for investment in new plantings
explanation: Names product, exact tariff change, and concrete beneficiaries.

text: Part of this agreement allows 1,670 high-skilled work visas to be issued to Indian nationals. These are targeted visas, designed to fill skills, and are not about opening the floodgates or changing the fabric of our communities.

text: Until now, India had a 50 percent tariff on imported apples; under the FTA, New Zealand apples get that cut to 25 percent within a quota, and over time that will come down.

text: coal is worth about $350-$450 million a year; the Indian market is worth an average of $150 million a year

text: After all, we cannot have solar farms and we cannot have solar panels and wind farms without coal.

text: Part of this agreement allows 1,670 high-skilled work visas to be issued to Indian nationals. These are targeted visas, designed to fill skills, and are not about opening the floodgates or changing the fabric of our communities.

text: Let's focus on the facts and not the fears. This is about complementing, not overwhelming, our workforce.

text: Our seafood is better than theirs; Indians deserve to eat it.

text: He does know what it's like to lose his seat. He had one in the Wairarapa and he lost it at the last election. ... Kieran McAnulty, who's actually given up on his ambition to lead the Labour Party at the moment because of a lack of policy.

text: We've come up with a solution to that. We're going to use a capital gains tax to pay for three free GP visits for everyone in the country.

text: I think it’s good that we’ve got a thoughtful party that is not yet convinced by this.

text: I’m sure the House will look forward to the contributions from the ACT Party as they try to explain themselves out of this little corner.
explanation: Combative point-scoring that alienates rather than persuades the party it targets.

text: without that advocacy over the years of all those people,”—all those people that we’ve mentioned here and the thousands of others that we haven’t directly named—“without their work, we wouldn’t be here. So yes, it does work. It really, really does.
explanation: Affirms that advocacy 'works' but offers no figures, mechanisms, or concrete causal detail — a warm but vague claim.

text: Country Road did their check, and they were horrified to find that their main sock supply did actually have a clear instance of modern slavery. They were able to address it because of the requirement on them of this kind of reporting.
explanation: Names the company and the specific supply-chain finding rather than speaking in generalities.

text: This bill will require reporting entities to report on how they identify, address, mitigate, and remediate incidents of modern slavery. It will require the Minister to report annually on progress towards combating modern slavery and to issue guidance on reporting suspected incidents of modern slavery processes that Government agencies should follow in response.
explanation: Precise, accurate summary of the bill's operative mechanisms — reporting duties, annual ministerial reporting, and guidance obligations.

text: why are we just looking at bigger companies when, actually, exploitation in the form of modern slavery can often happen within small businesses and it could often happen in other circumstances which are not part of the supply chain?
explanation: Names the gap (small businesses, non-supply-chain settings) but does not propose a concrete alternative threshold or mechanism.

text: there is going to be a two-year review period. Maybe the House got it wrong and we'll know that within two years. So, possibly, adjustments could be made at that two-year period.
explanation: Names a concrete two-year review mechanism and its purpose.

text: I love it when we have “Kumbaya” moments in this House—that’s why I love Treaty settlement days most of all—but we are a debating chamber for good reason. When we debate things and we debate them well and we debate them faithfully, we actually get better law and we get better policy.
explanation: Respects the dissenting ACT party's right to debate and frames disagreement as productive rather than as bad faith.

text: I think it’s good that we’ve got a thoughtful party that is not yet convinced by this.
explanation: Characterises the lone dissenting party (ACT) as 'thoughtful' rather than attacking them — respectful of an opponent.

text: I particularly want to thank Laura McClure for her very thoughtful comments.
explanation: Direct, respectful acknowledgement of the opposing speaker's critique despite disagreement.

text: Good on Greg Fleming and good on Camilla Belich for going around Brooke van Velden, who has been very busy in the area of workplace relations, doing all the wrong things, eroding workplace relations here, there, and everywhere.
explanation: Sweeping personal swipe at van Velden ('doing all the wrong things') with no specific policy substance — character/competence attack rather than engaged critique.

text: I’m sure the House will look forward to the contributions from the ACT Party as they try to explain themselves out of this little corner.
explanation: Taunting, pre-emptive mockery of ACT rather than engaging the substance of their objections.

text: there is going to be a two-year review period. Maybe the House got it wrong and we'll know that within two years. So, possibly, adjustments could be made at that two-year period.
explanation: Humble, open acknowledgement that the House might be wrong; constructive tone.

text: That’s why, in my opening remarks, I mentioned my friend Selwyn Coles’ Master’s thesis and the work he did for that year at Oxford, really wrestling with that question—does this work?—and actually looking at dozens and hundreds of contacts around the world. His thoughtful conclusion was that, yes, it would add real value here in New Zealand. It was that work that persuaded me to push on with it.
explanation: Grounds his support in research rather than mere conviction, and concedes he was initially unpersuaded; relies on a single thesis as authority, so evidence is cited but not independently weighed.

text: Country Road did their check, and they were horrified to find that their main sock supply did actually have a clear instance of modern slavery. They were able to address it because of the requirement on them of this kind of reporting.
explanation: Uses a concrete real-world case to support the claim that reporting requirements drive remediation; one illustrative anecdote rather than systematic evidence.

text: why are we just looking at bigger companies when, actually, exploitation in the form of modern slavery can often happen within small businesses and it could often happen in other circumstances which are not part of the supply chain?
explanation: Identifies a genuine scope gap (exploitation outside large-company supply chains) as a reasoned critique of the bill's coverage.

text: We were given assurances, actually, that the people or, at least, the skill sets in those other two organisations will be migrated over into DIA, so some of the concerns that people have—well, actually, an organisation like the Reserve Bank has a very specific skill set and so do folks within the FMA, so knowing that those skill sets will be migrated over into DIA is a source of comfort.
explanation: Addresses a genuine risk (loss of specialist expertise) and explains why the assurance mitigates it.

text: when I was managing a school bus company, I observed students in some remote communities, and some not so remote communities, who were kept out of school for various reasons, not travelling on the school bus when they should’ve been, who were then being, in some cases, used by their parents to work in spaces, whether they were illegal or not, for no employment.
explanation: First-hand observation broadening the scope of 'modern slavery' to domestic child labour; a personal anecdote, persuasive but not systematic evidence.

text: That’s why, in my opening remarks, I mentioned my friend Selwyn Coles’ Master’s thesis and the work he did for that year at Oxford, really wrestling with that question—does this work?—and actually looking at dozens and hundreds of contacts around the world. His thoughtful conclusion was that, yes, it would add real value here in New Zealand. It was that work that persuaded me to push on with it.
explanation: Candidly admits he was not immediately convinced and explains what changed his mind — a transparent account of his own position shift.

text: I think, before all of this, I probably was one of those people that thought this does not exist on our New Zealand shores.
explanation: Candidly admits her own prior misconception and credits advocacy with changing her mind — a transparent, self-aware account rather than a claim of consistent virtue.

text: having sat on the board of a company in Australia that was required by the Australian legislation to report under their version of what will soon be law here in New Zealand. It is a conversation that occurs around that table, of “Have we gone far enough visiting the factory in Vietnam? Do we actually know X, Y, or Z from that part of our supply chain in Europe?”
explanation: His cautious, cost-aware stance is backed by his own lived experience administering the equivalent law.

text: Country Road did their check, and they were horrified to find that their main sock supply did actually have a clear instance of modern slavery. They were able to address it because of the requirement on them of this kind of reporting.
explanation: Factual claim about a specific company's disclosure; broadly consistent with reported Australian modern-slavery cases, though details are second-hand.

text: the 2023 Global Survey Index recognised that there would be approximately 8,000 people living in modern slavery in New Zealand. That’s 8,000 people living on our shores who are living in the most horrific and horrendous conditions that we could imagine.
explanation: The ~8,000 NZ figure matches the 2023 Global Slavery Index (slightly misnamed 'Global Survey Index'); core claim accurate.

text: we have bypassed the ballot and we have used the Standing Order for the first time that enables this bill to go straight to first reading and then through to select committee.
explanation: Factual procedural claim consistent with other speakers noting this was the first use of Standing Order 288 for such a bill.

text: we know that the current mayor, Wayne Brown, is a very strong-minded mayor. He gets the final say, and so I'm sure that if he consults with the governing body and they don't agree, I have a feeling that he won't care much and he will put on to the committee the people whom he thinks are the best.
explanation: Prediction the mayor will override the governing body; plausible characterisation but speculative.

text: what concerns me with this bill, with its focus on Auckland—creates a bespoke solution for Auckland Transport—is that, actually, we'll see more and more funding going to Auckland and the transport system in Auckland, and therefore other cities across New Zealand will miss out on that needed funding.
explanation: Predicts the bill will divert funding from other cities to Auckland; a contested causal forecast not strongly evidenced.

text: We were given assurances, actually, that the people or, at least, the skill sets in those other two organisations will be migrated over into DIA, so some of the concerns that people have—well, actually, an organisation like the Reserve Bank has a very specific skill set and so do folks within the FMA, so knowing that those skill sets will be migrated over into DIA is a source of comfort.
explanation: Reports assurances given in committee about skill transfer; accurate as a report, though the outcome is unverified.

text: while my party, Te Pāti Māori, supports this bill, we will not let these issues fade. We will monitor implementation closely. We will push for stronger Māori representation. We will advocate for Te Tiriti - consistent planning, for the protection of Māori land and cultural sites, and for transparent reporting of Māori outcomes.
explanation: Clear stated commitments to monitor and advocate, but these are future intentions with no delivery yet shown.

text: By allowing people to have appropriate businesses on conservation land and to charge visiting tourists to go there, we can all go and enjoy these special places, and we can also build things like toilets, which are required, because it’s a hell of a lot better to have toilets than people wandering behind the bushes.
explanation: Names a mechanism (businesses/charging tourists fund facilities) but no figures or detail on safeguards.

text: Last weekend, on Sunday, on the way back from the dairy awards evening in Rotorua, I dropped into the Maungatautari sanctuary and had a look round. It’s just an amazing, amazing thing that’s happened there; the locals have done a lot of great work.
explanation: Anchored to a named place and event but a general impression rather than detailed claims.

text: It’s very short bill. It’s a simple bill.
explanation: Vague characterisation with no concrete content.

text: One statistic they shared was particularly striking: 92.9 percent of parents surveyed said they had little to no idea how to keep their children safe online.
explanation: Precise figure attributed to a named source.

text: That is why I believe recommendation 3.10 in this report is one of the most important recommendations. The committee recommends that the Government invest in public online safety campaigns and better resources to educate and empower parents, caregivers, and young people.
explanation: Names a specific recommendation and its content, though stops short of funding amounts or timeframe.

text: Here we have 588 submissions. Again, they are almost unanimous in saying we don’t want this.
explanation: Gives the exact submission count and the direction of submitter sentiment.

text: We know that it matters more, because we know from the Ministry for the Environment’s own work that environmental outcomes across the spectrum—whether it be air, water, ocean, or biodiversity—are going backwards.
explanation: Names the domains (air, water, ocean, biodiversity) but not specific indicators or figures.

text: Bronwyn Hayward from University of Canterbury has pointed out that the assurances in the Cabinet paper that say that stakeholders may fear environmental priorities will be diluted and these concerns are unfounded because other countries successfully integrate similar functions—she could find “no evidence of other countries that have successfully integrated such diverse oversight as Environment” with development and economic objectives. The only ones she could find were the Maldives and Kosovo, which have really unfortunate and concerning conflict of interest issues.
explanation: Names the expert, the comparison, and the only countervailing examples (Maldives, Kosovo).

text: I want to make it clear to New Zealanders that the disestablishment of their ministry—the Ministry for the Environment—occurred with just over three hours of consideration from the Environment Committee, and that included the time for public hearings. We had just two hours and 45 minutes of public hearings, where, again, everyone was telling us that it was a bad idea and they didn’t want it to happen.
explanation: Exact durations for committee consideration and public hearings.

text: Look, on the side of the House, we are progressive. You can achieve development as well as protecting the environment at the same time.
explanation: General claim with no mechanism for how development and protection coexist.

text: This bill is structural, it’s administrative, and it is the first step to creating the Ministry of Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport—MCERT—and, of course, this is going to support housing, transport, urban development, environment, climate adaptation, housing affordability, infrastructure, and protecting our environment at the same time.
explanation: Names the new ministry and a list of domains, but the 'will support' claims have no mechanism or evidence.

text: Look, our conservation land makes up a third of New Zealand, and it's time for us to manage our conservation estate more efficiently and better... The current Conservation Act is almost 40 years old. It's out of date, and it is time for change.
explanation: Concrete on scale and age but general on the change itself.

text: In December, almost 5 million social media account were disestablished in the first few days, and it’s been successful.
explanation: Gives a concrete figure and timeframe.

text: I will point to the submission by the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment (PCE), Simon Upton... there is a “real risk with this ‘mega-ministry’ that the trade-offs will [now] be resolved within the organisation” by officials, whereas they should have been and should be elevated to ministerial decision-making where the accountability for those trade-offs will sit.
explanation: Names the PCE and the specific concern about internal vs ministerial resolution of trade-offs.

text: This bill was introduced on 15 February, it had its first reading on 19 February, it opened for submissions on 20 February, and less than two weeks, when it comes to business days, was what people had to submit on a bill that will disestablish an important ministry. We had less than three hours of hearings, and bear in mind we had 588 submissions—
explanation: Exact introduction/reading/submission dates, submission window, hearing time and submission count.

text: This Government's track record when it comes to protecting the environment is appalling. What they've just done is the process of disestablishing the Ministry for the Environment; cutting a significant amount of funding for conservation; replacing that with funding from the International Visitor Levy (IVL)... amending the Conservation Act to put economic growth ahead of protecting the environment.
explanation: Names specific moves: disestablishing the Ministry, conservation funding cuts, IVL substitution, Conservation Act amendment, RMA replacement.

text: By allowing people to have appropriate businesses on conservation land and to charge visiting tourists to go there, we can all go and enjoy these special places, and we can also build things like toilets, which are required, because it’s a hell of a lot better to have toilets than people wandering behind the bushes.
explanation: Argues the case without attacking opponents.

text: Last weekend, on Sunday, on the way back from the dairy awards evening in Rotorua, I dropped into the Maungatautari sanctuary and had a look round. It’s just an amazing, amazing thing that’s happened there; the locals have done a lot of great work.
explanation: Warm, generous acknowledgement of community conservation work; no conflict.

text: I want to really acknowledge the significant amount of work the select committee did, particularly the leadership of acting chair Carl Bates and the lead Opposition member, the Hon Phil Twyford. It was a very constructive and cohesive process.
explanation: Respectful acknowledgement across party lines.

text: We heard a member opposite talking about tourists having to pay to partake in the beauty of New Zealand’s nature—and, sure, I don’t disagree with that, so long as that money is spent on the upkeep of things like tracks, protecting our native species and areas, not funding restaurants and wine bars in the most pristine areas of our conservation estate.
explanation: Largely substance-focused, though the 'wine bars in pristine areas' framing edges toward caricature.

text: I want to make it clear to New Zealanders that the disestablishment of their ministry—the Ministry for the Environment—occurred with just over three hours of consideration from the Environment Committee, and that included the time for public hearings. We had just two hours and 45 minutes of public hearings, where, again, everyone was telling us that it was a bad idea and they didn’t want it to happen.
explanation: Critical but focused on process facts rather than personal attack.

text: This is an absolute travesty for New Zealand, and this Government should be absolutely ashamed of themselves.
explanation: Hyperbolic condemnation ('absolute travesty', 'should be ashamed') aimed at the Government collectively.

text: At a time when we are going through a climate crisis, a biodiversity crisis, and we have the highest level of threatened species in the world, her Government is pushing through bills that will again weaken and water down environmental protections as she rushes them through select committee, and yet she thinks this is common sense.
explanation: Sharp but argues against the policy and the chair's process, not her character.

text: This Government's track record when it comes to protecting the environment is appalling. What they've just done is the process of disestablishing the Ministry for the Environment; cutting a significant amount of funding for conservation; replacing that with funding from the International Visitor Levy (IVL)... amending the Conservation Act to put economic growth ahead of protecting the environment.
explanation: 'Appalling' is harsh, but the criticism targets policies and the Government's record with a list of actions, not personal attacks on individuals.

text: By allowing people to have appropriate businesses on conservation land and to charge visiting tourists to go there, we can all go and enjoy these special places, and we can also build things like toilets, which are required, because it’s a hell of a lot better to have toilets than people wandering behind the bushes.
explanation: Has a clear means-ends logic (revenue funds facilities) but leans on a vivid anecdotal contrast rather than data.

text: It’s very short bill. It’s a simple bill.
explanation: Minimising interjection; asserts simplicity as a reason to dismiss concerns without supporting it.

text: After all, we accept common-sense protections around risks for children in the physical world: think about things like how we require seat belts in cars, we fence swimming pools, and we regulate harmful products like alcohol. The online environment should not be exempt from the same common-sense thinking simply because it is digital.
explanation: Argument by analogy to existing safety regulation; intuitively appealing but leans on the analogy rather than evidence that online regulation works comparably.

text: The bill will enable the department to use and develop “to the greatest extent”—what does that mean? It is very ambiguous.
explanation: Legitimately flags vague statutory wording, though stops at raising the question rather than analysing it.

text: Not one party campaigned on the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment, because if they had, they would not be in Government.
explanation: The causal 'because they would not be in Government' is an unfalsifiable counterfactual presented as fact.

text: We know that it matters more, because we know from the Ministry for the Environment’s own work that environmental outcomes across the spectrum—whether it be air, water, ocean, or biodiversity—are going backwards.
explanation: Grounds the claim in a named evidence source (MfE's own reporting) and the conclusion follows.

text: Bronwyn Hayward from University of Canterbury has pointed out that the assurances in the Cabinet paper that say that stakeholders may fear environmental priorities will be diluted and these concerns are unfounded because other countries successfully integrate similar functions—she could find “no evidence of other countries that have successfully integrated such diverse oversight as Environment” with development and economic objectives. The only ones she could find were the Maldives and Kosovo, which have really unfortunate and concerning conflict of interest issues.
explanation: Cites a named academic and a specific evidentiary finding to rebut the Cabinet paper's claim.

text: I will point to the submission by the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment (PCE), Simon Upton... there is a “real risk with this ‘mega-ministry’ that the trade-offs will [now] be resolved within the organisation” by officials, whereas they should have been and should be elevated to ministerial decision-making where the accountability for those trade-offs will sit.
explanation: Builds on a named, authoritative submission and a clear mechanism (where trade-offs and accountability are resolved).

text: I will speak to my experience when Labour was in Government and established the Ministry for Ethnic Communities, elevating it from an office that sat within the Department of Internal Affairs... so that independent policy advice pertaining to those matters would actually see the light of day and would not be subsumed in a mega-ministry. This bill is taking us in the opposite direction.
explanation: Reasoned analogy with a relevant precedent, though the parallel is asserted rather than fully demonstrated.

text: This Government's track record when it comes to protecting the environment is appalling. What they've just done is the process of disestablishing the Ministry for the Environment; cutting a significant amount of funding for conservation; replacing that with funding from the International Visitor Levy (IVL)... amending the Conservation Act to put economic growth ahead of protecting the environment.
explanation: Backs the strong conclusion ('appalling track record') by enumerating specific concrete actions as evidence rather than mere assertion.

text: I take the Minister's point that there's no massive change—or “any change”, I think, is what the Minister said—to risk thresholds per se. But in trying to speed up the process, if the checks and balances aren't there to ensure the appropriate management of these substances and new organisms, then there is a risk there.
explanation: Conditional reasoning that concedes the stated position then identifies the specific contingency (loss of checks and balances) under which risk arises.

text: Look, on the side of the House, we are progressive. You can achieve development as well as protecting the environment at the same time.
explanation: Offers a both-things framing but mostly asserts her side's position rather than reaching across.

text: We have guardrails in the physical world to protect our young children, but we have no guardrails in the online world. It’s high time we do. We have a drinking age. We have a driving age. We should also have a social media age.
explanation: Confident and resonant framing, though it appeals chiefly to those already sympathetic.

text: Today marks a significant moment in this House, as we work across parties on this very important issue: to protect our kids from online harm... This is bigger than politics; this is bigger than this House. The future of our kids is too important to get this wrong.
explanation: Frames the issue as above partisanship and welcomes cross-party work — unifying.

text: The Prime Minister promised all New Zealanders that he would fix the cost of living, but nothing is getting better.
explanation: 'Nothing is getting better' is an absolute, unsupported characterisation; cost-of-living indicators are mixed, not uniformly static.

text: Given what we know from this piece of legislation, that it allows the Minister to sell off—or get rid of; sorry—conservation land as he sees fit, it gives the Minister a heck of a lot of powers and all New Zealanders should be concerned.
explanation: Characterises the bill as letting the Minister sell land 'as he sees fit', an overstatement of the discretionary powers as described.

text: Here we have 588 submissions. Again, they are almost unanimous in saying we don’t want this.
explanation: The 588 figure is corroborated by Priyanca Radhakrishnan; the near-unanimity claim is supported by repeated accounts of submissions opposing the bill.

text: Not one party campaigned on the disestablishment of the Ministry for the Environment, because if they had, they would not be in Government.
explanation: The factual core—no party campaigned on disestablishing the ministry—is plausible and unrebutted, though hard to verify exhaustively.

text: We know that it matters more, because we know from the Ministry for the Environment’s own work that environmental outcomes across the spectrum—whether it be air, water, ocean, or biodiversity—are going backwards.
explanation: MfE environmental reporting does document declines across several domains, broadly supporting the claim.

text: I want to make it clear to New Zealanders that the disestablishment of their ministry—the Ministry for the Environment—occurred with just over three hours of consideration from the Environment Committee, and that included the time for public hearings. We had just two hours and 45 minutes of public hearings, where, again, everyone was telling us that it was a bad idea and they didn’t want it to happen.
explanation: Precise process figures consistent with Radhakrishnan's 'less than three hours of hearings' account.

text: At a time when we are going through a climate crisis, a biodiversity crisis, and we have the highest level of threatened species in the world, her Government is pushing through bills that will again weaken and water down environmental protections as she rushes them through select committee, and yet she thinks this is common sense.
explanation: NZ has one of the highest proportions of threatened species, but 'highest level in the world' is an overstatement of a contested ranking.

text: This bill was introduced on 15 February, it had its first reading on 19 February, it opened for submissions on 20 February, and less than two weeks, when it comes to business days, was what people had to submit on a bill that will disestablish an important ministry. We had less than three hours of hearings, and bear in mind we had 588 submissions—
explanation: Precise dates and figures consistent with other members' accounts of the truncated process.

text: This Government's track record when it comes to protecting the environment is appalling. What they've just done is the process of disestablishing the Ministry for the Environment; cutting a significant amount of funding for conservation; replacing that with funding from the International Visitor Levy (IVL)... amending the Conservation Act to put economic growth ahead of protecting the environment.
explanation: The listed actions broadly correspond to real coalition-Government measures, though framed advocately ('put economic growth ahead'); directionally accurate.

text: Most will know that I’ve been part of the seabed mining kaupapa and the opposition to what we don’t want to happen in our environment—for 15 years in fact—and when you get down to the crux of it, when you get down to winning in the High Court, to winning in the Court of Appeal, to winning in the Supreme Court, they all came down to the role of what iwi and Te Tiriti had in that aspect.
explanation: Points to a long, consistent 15-year personal record of opposing seabed mining—words backed by a documented track record.

text: I will speak to my experience when Labour was in Government and established the Ministry for Ethnic Communities, elevating it from an office that sat within the Department of Internal Affairs... so that independent policy advice pertaining to those matters would actually see the light of day and would not be subsumed in a mega-ministry. This bill is taking us in the opposite direction.
explanation: Draws on her own party's consistent prior action (elevating Ethnic Communities to a ministry) to ground today's opposition.

text: We will indeed be opposing this, and when we get back into Government, we’ll fix this righteous mess they have made.
explanation: Vague future commitment to 'fix' contingent on returning to government, with no mechanism or detail.

text: This bill is structural, it’s administrative, and it is the first step to creating the Ministry of Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport—MCERT—and, of course, this is going to support housing, transport, urban development, environment, climate adaptation, housing affordability, infrastructure, and protecting our environment at the same time.
explanation: Broad promise that one structural change will deliver across many areas, asserted rather than demonstrated.

text: Last year, with support of our National Party caucus and our Prime Minister and education Minister, I introduced my member’s bill to ban social media for under-16s. It’s great to stand here today and see this work progressed.
explanation: Concrete action taken (introduced a member's bill) now reflected in committee work; delivery in progress rather than fully enacted.

text: I have received no official advice on the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs. That sits under the auspices of the Minister for Social Development and Employment.
explanation: Direct, clear answer to what advice he has received.

text: In terms of the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs, my understanding is that the funding hasn't been cut, but there has been a reallocation of resources to areas in greater need... the member is looking at this through far too narrow a prism; you've got to look at the wider work programme that the Government's doing.
explanation: Disputes the premise of a cut and answers partly, then redirects to the wider programme.

text: I can assure the member that I'm a staunch advocate for the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs. I have a peripheral involvement with the Clutha District in the Jobbortunities initiative there; I do know that it works.
explanation: Affirms support but again pivots to the fast-track jobs argument rather than concrete steps.

text: Te Pāti Māori's support for changes to section 4 is conditional on broad support by te iwi Māori on proposed changes made with iwi Māori, while acknowledging the independent voices of whānau, hapū, and iwi, who may take different positions.
explanation: States a clear, conditional party position.

text: —in the disposals and swap process, and they are not unilateral, Priyanca Radhakrishnan... there is a process which is set out there and it's quite an extensive process... Labour is not interested in the submissions—it's already made its mind up—but I'm looking forward to the submissions and seeing what New Zealanders have to say.
explanation: Addresses the unilateral-disposal concern directly.

text: Look, our conservation land makes up a third of New Zealand, and it's time for us to manage our conservation estate more efficiently and better... The current Conservation Act is almost 40 years old. It's out of date, and it is time for change.
explanation: DOC manages roughly a third of NZ's land and the Act dates to 1987—both broadly accurate.

text: In December, almost 5 million social media account were disestablished in the first few days, and it’s been successful.
explanation: Cites a specific figure on Australia's ban and asserts success; the number is plausible but unsourced and 'successful' is an early, contestable judgement.

text: In terms of the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs, my understanding is that the funding hasn't been cut, but there has been a reallocation of resources to areas in greater need... the member is looking at this through far too narrow a prism; you've got to look at the wider work programme that the Government's doing.
explanation: Argues 'reallocation not cut' but mostly reframes rather than addressing the Kaikōura-specific reduction cited.

text: I am aware of the enormous surge in confidence in our farming community... The broader primary sector, with $60 billion-odd of exports, is going really well, and that is, I think, probably attributed to a suite of Government policies. Particularly, I think I'd look to the Resource Management Act reform.
explanation: Attributes the confidence surge to Government policy ('probably') without isolating causes.

text: I know of the dicyandiamide issue that Fonterra had with what was a compound additive to fertiliser; it ended up in the food chain, and it was incredibly disruptive to our markets in Asia in particular—those critical markets.
explanation: Uses a real historical case as evidence that streamlining must retain rigour, supporting his cautionary conclusion with a relevant precedent.

text: Everywhere else in the world, you pay to see the sights, you pay to see the attractions, and you should do the same here in New Zealand so that we can use that money and put it back into improving and protecting our environment and biodiversity.
explanation: 'Everywhere else in the world' is an overgeneralised appeal to analogy supporting the charging policy.

text: We have guardrails in the physical world to protect our young children, but we have no guardrails in the online world. It’s high time we do. We have a drinking age. We have a driving age. We should also have a social media age.
explanation: Argument by analogy to age-gated activities; rhetorically tidy but relies on the analogy rather than evidence the analogy holds online.

text: I was recently in Australia and saw the successful, positive impact of their ban for under-16s on social media.
explanation: Relies on personal anecdote ('I saw') to assert a policy's success rather than outcome data.

text: I can assure the member that I'm a staunch advocate for the Mayors' Taskforce for Jobs. I have a peripheral involvement with the Clutha District in the Jobbortunities initiative there; I do know that it works.
explanation: Professes to be a 'staunch advocate' while accepting funding has been reoriented and saying it isn't his portfolio—words sit in some tension with the described changes.

text: We will be scrutinising this, and we hope there will be a full select committee process, because this is a very important bill but we don't want this to be a stalking horse for doing some other things that it's not necessarily intended to do.
explanation: A coalition partner publicly flagging it will scrutinise its own Government's bill; a stated commitment to oversight with no visible action yet to confirm it.

text: This month, we are conducting a major foot-and-mouth disease preparedness exercise in Taranaki: operation “Farm Gate”... New Zealand has never had a case of foot-and-mouth disease, but if we did, it would cost this country around $15 billion in lost exports... and in destroyed herds and flocks.
explanation: Describes an active readiness exercise underway, building on a signed industry agreement.

text: We have the toughest biosecurity border protection in the world. But risk can never be zero... well-established readiness and response plans have helped us to eradicate four separate incursions of fruit fly during this term of Government.
explanation: Points to four eradications delivered this term as evidence of capability.

text: The response team has now captured and identified over 4,500 exotic hornets, but none has been found since 2 April, and no nests have been found since late March... The Government has been determined in its intention to eradicate yellow-legged hornets and supported it with an investment of $12 million.
explanation: Reports concrete progress on a funded eradication effort.

text: This bill is a great example of how Government is making real regulatory change that will benefit farming businesses and the wider primary sector. I commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Claims delivery of 'real regulatory change' for a bill only at first reading and not yet enacted; intent and announcement rather than demonstrated follow-through.

text: Our forces are working hard towards becoming an increasingly integrated combat capable Anzac force, integrated by 2035.
explanation: Forecasts an integrated Anzac force by 2035; a plausible long-term goal but a decade out and dependent on policy continuity.

text: The response team has now captured and identified over 4,500 exotic hornets, but none has been found since 2 April, and no nests have been found since late March... The Government has been determined in its intention to eradicate yellow-legged hornets and supported it with an investment of $12 million.
explanation: Implicitly forecasts likely eradication success ('looking promising'); cautiously hedged with 'fingers crossed'.

text: I want to really acknowledge the significant amount of work the select committee did, particularly the leadership of acting chair Carl Bates and the lead Opposition member, the Hon Phil Twyford. It was a very constructive and cohesive process.
explanation: Credits an Opposition member by name and praises a cohesive cross-party process — bridge-building.

text: In the final 10 seconds that I have, moving forward, we need to include young people in the conversation and the design of the solutions to address this issue, which is all about them.
explanation: Inclusive call to bring affected young people into solution design; unifying though general.

text: I believe that we need to have a little bit of faith in our youth sometimes. They are actually smart and they understand the potential harm online, and they have the resilience to navigate those challenges. I think we just need to give them a little bit of guidance and education.
explanation: Inclusive, optimistic framing that brings young people in rather than positioning them only as victims.

text: Maybe it is time for all of us to reflect on our own habits. Maybe it is time for us to put down our cell phones a little bit more often, spend more time with our children, listen to them... no technology will replace the guidance, love, and people of our family.
explanation: Universal, self-including appeal to shared family values; unifying but soft.

text: I also want to highlight the new powers given to the New Zealand Transport Agency Waka Kotahi to close unsafe highways. I think that this is a really good safety move. It’s a common-sense measure. When a road is unsafe due to weather damage or other risks, the regulator is able to act quickly to protect people.
explanation: Praises a Government measure from the Opposition benches — credits the other side where she agrees.

text: Today marks a significant moment in this House, as we work across parties on this very important issue: to protect our kids from online harm... This is bigger than politics; this is bigger than this House. The future of our kids is too important to get this wrong.
explanation: Collegial and respectful, no opponents targeted.

text: However, there’s a large hole in this bill, in that it does not tackle the bigger issues around transport and affordability, emissions reduction, or public transport accessibility. The Government had an opportunity to consider a wider remit as part of this amendment, and they have chosen not to.
explanation: Criticises the bill's scope and the Government's choice on policy grounds, no personal attack.

text: The bill allows infringement notices and reminders to be served electronically... It also enables electronic warrants of fitness, certificates of fitness, and certificates of loading.
explanation: Lists specific mechanisms the bill enables, naming the document types affected.

text: We went through a tunnel in the Kaimais that hasn’t had a passenger rail train go through it in 14 years... We’re connecting Auckland, Hamilton, and Tauranga, the “golden triangle”, with public transport options. At a time when fuel prices are increasing, now is the time to make that change and to invest in more public transport.
explanation: Names a concrete route and rationale (golden triangle, rising fuel prices) though the 'invest more' ask lacks figures or timeline.

text: I also want to highlight the new powers given to the New Zealand Transport Agency Waka Kotahi to close unsafe highways. I think that this is a really good safety move. It’s a common-sense measure. When a road is unsafe due to weather damage or other risks, the regulator is able to act quickly to protect people.
explanation: Identifies the specific power and its trigger (weather/road risk) though stays at description level.

text: The bill is a modernisation bill. It is bringing us to a digitalised driver’s licence, which I look forward to. I commend this bill to the House.
explanation: Identifies the bill's core purpose (digital licence) but offers little detail beyond it.

text: I believe that having a bill or a piece of legislation that simply introduces an age limit is not going far enough, not doing enough to actually address the real harms that many have spoken to us about.
explanation: Consistent with Labour's stated preference for a multi-recommendation approach over a single age limit.

text: Last year, with support of our National Party caucus and our Prime Minister and education Minister, I introduced my member’s bill to ban social media for under-16s. It’s great to stand here today and see this work progressed.
explanation: Her advocacy today is consistent with the bill she introduced — words and record align.

text: I think there’s a lot assumption that parents know. I would hold the view that a lot of parents don’t know. They’ve never grown up with the technology. They’ve never had the ability to use the technology.
explanation: Reasonable generational point supporting the case for parent education, but rests on personal observation rather than data (though it echoes the 92.9% survey cited earlier).

text: However, there’s a large hole in this bill, in that it does not tackle the bigger issues around transport and affordability, emissions reduction, or public transport accessibility. The Government had an opportunity to consider a wider remit as part of this amendment, and they have chosen not to.
explanation: Identifies specific omitted areas (affordability, emissions, accessibility), a substantive critique, though it doesn't evidence the impact of the omission.

text: We went through a tunnel in the Kaimais that hasn’t had a passenger rail train go through it in 14 years... We’re connecting Auckland, Hamilton, and Tauranga, the “golden triangle”, with public transport options. At a time when fuel prices are increasing, now is the time to make that change and to invest in more public transport.
explanation: Links rising fuel prices to a public-transport case; reasonable but leans on an anecdotal train trip rather than data.

text: One statistic they shared was particularly striking: 92.9 percent of parents surveyed said they had little to no idea how to keep their children safe online.
explanation: Cites a specific survey figure from Our Kids Online; plausible and precisely stated, but the underlying survey's representativeness is unverified.

text: The bill allows infringement notices and reminders to be served electronically... It also enables electronic warrants of fitness, certificates of fitness, and certificates of loading.
explanation: Accurate, checkable description of the bill's digitisation provisions.

text: We bought The Worst Children’s Library to this Parliament, and I did that with a colleague from the National Party. That was a deliberate attempt to make sure that this was not politicised in an unhealthy way. We let those from all the parties who had brought member’s bills on these issues, speak at that event.
explanation: Describes a concrete, delivered action (bringing the exhibit to Parliament and hosting a cross-party event), not just an aspiration.

text: I'm rather disappointed to hear my colleague Steve Abel there. I thought we almost had him in supporting, but never mind. Hopefully we can get him back.
explanation: Good-humoured and respectful toward an opponent — expresses disappointment without any personal attack and keeps the door open.

text: This bill cuts unnecessary bureaucracy and red tape. Trusting credible overseas regulators like Australia, the UK, Canada, and the US is smart. It's about delivering for our farmers and growers. We are fixing the basics and building the future for our rock star primary producers.
explanation: Assertions that the approach is 'smart' with no supporting evidence or reasoning offered.

text: I take the Minister's point that there's no massive change—or “any change”, I think, is what the Minister said—to risk thresholds per se. But in trying to speed up the process, if the checks and balances aren't there to ensure the appropriate management of these substances and new organisms, then there is a risk there.
explanation: Acknowledges and fairly restates the Minister's point before registering her own concern — engages rather than dismisses.

text: OK, have a look at this external consultation list. I just read it out to you. The SPCA wasn't on it, and no veterinary organisation was on that list. Given it's veterinary medicines, it seems a strange omission.
explanation: Directly answers Miles Anderson's challenge ('It is a consultation, isn't it, Steve?') by pointing to the actual consultation list and identifying who is missing.

text: This is all about fixing the basics so that build a future for Kiwi families, Kiwi families that could be moving into their own house today but have been stopped by rules that are onerous and put unnecessary obligations particularly on lenders.
explanation: Aspirational framing about enabling families to build homes; states intent behind the bill but describes no delivered outcome, so it is announcement/aspiration rather than demonstrated follow-through.

text: We are not producing enough babies in this country to ensure that we have a stable or even growing population. We are going to rely on migration... We will have a declining population if it isn’t for smart, skilled immigration
explanation: Predicts a declining population absent migration — directionally supported by current fertility/demographic data.

text: The move to a single supervisor in the Department of Internal Affairs will mean clearer accountability, faster guidance, and more reliable support for businesses who are trying to comply with the law. The transition is on track to go live on 1 July 2026
explanation: Forecasts the transition will go live on schedule and improve accountability — plausible but a prediction about delivery.
